q: What is the regulatory classification of the FOM?
a: It is classified as an FAA-accepted manual with approved content.

src.quote: The FOM is classified as an FAA-accepted manual with approved content.
src.note: The FOM is an accepted manual, but portions of its content are FAA-approved. Publication follows the FAA Approval/Acceptance Request Process defined in the Company Administrative Manual.

q: Per the FOM, who has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance in the interest of safety, and under which regulations?
a: The PIC, as set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557.

src.quote: As set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557, the PIC has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety.
src.note: The manual cannot anticipate every situation, so the PIC retains deviation authority scoped to what safety requires.

q: If a conflict exists between Company manuals, what hierarchy applies?
a: F&F/Company NOTAMs, then Required Operational Memos, then 10-7 information.

src.quote: If a conflict exists between Company manuals, the following hierarchy applies:
src.note: The listed order ranks the sources: F&F/Company NOTAMs are highest, followed by Required Operational Memos, then 10-7 information.

q: When manual guidance conflicts, which guidance governs?
a: The more restrictive guidance will apply.

src.quote: In the event of conflicting manual guidance, the more restrictive guidance will apply.
src.note: This 'most restrictive wins' rule also reappears in 1.5 for conflicting directives across the Company Manual System.

q: How are incremental revisions to the FOM numbered?
a: They are numbered subsequent to the current revision (e.g., 123.1, 123.2) until the next full revision (e.g., 124, 125).

src.quote: An incremental revision will be numbered subsequent to the current revision (e.g., 123.1, 123.2) until the next full revision (e.g., 124, 125), and will retain the change bars from the current full revision.
src.note: Incremental revisions push out information earlier than a full revision allows, or for content with a specific effective date, and keep the current full revision's change bars.

q: By what means are changes to regulatory information conveyed to crews?
a: By Required Operational Memo, Field & Facility (F&F)/Company NOTAMs, and Manual Revision or Incremental Revision.

src.quote: Alaska Airlines is responsible for timely dissemination of all regulatory information required for safe, compliant flight operations.
src.note: Regulatory changes use those three channels; administrative information instead goes out by Informational Memo and Company email.

q: In the FOM's conventions, what do the words 'Shall' or 'Must' indicate?
a: That a procedure, practice, or condition is mandatory.

src.quote: “Shall” or “Must” indicates that a procedure, practice, or condition is mandatory.
src.note: By contrast 'Should' means recommended, and 'May' or 'Need not' means optional.

q: What does the word 'Should' indicate in this manual, versus 'May' or 'Need not'?
a: 'Should' indicates a procedure, practice, or condition is recommended; 'May' or 'Need not' indicates it is optional.

src.quote: “Should” indicates that a procedure, practice, or condition is recommended.
src.note: Three tiers: mandatory (Shall/Must), recommended (Should), optional (May/Need not).

q: What is the difference between a WARNING and a CAUTION in the FOM?
a: A WARNING flags a procedure, practice, or condition that may result in injury or death; a CAUTION flags one that may result in damage to equipment.

src.quote: An operating procedure, practice, or condition that may result in injury or death if not carefully observed or followed.
src.note: WARNING is about people (injury or death); CAUTION is about equipment damage; a Note simply adds emphasis or explanation.

q: What are the three phases of the 'Ready, SAFE, Go' model?
a: Am I Ready?, Is Everything SAFE?, and Can I Go?

src.quote: This phase focuses on your preparation. Before you act, ensure you are ready and have the right resources.
src.note: Ready = preparation and resources; SAFE = self-assess for hazards and act to prevent adverse outcomes; Go = proceed with a safety focus without rushing.

q: What are the four pillars of Alaska's SMS?
a: Safety Policy, Safety Risk Management, Safety Assurance, and Safety Promotion.

src.quote: A process within our SMS that describes a system, identifies any associated hazards, and analyzes, assesses, and controls risk to as low as reasonably practicable.
src.note: Safety Risk Management controls risk to as low as reasonably practicable; the four pillars together form the SMS framework.

q: Who owns the SMS at AAG, and who are the named Accountable Executives?
a: The AAG Accountable Executives own the SMS: Jason Berry (AS, COO) for Alaska Airlines and Andy Schneider (QX, CEO/President) for Horizon Air.

src.quote: The AAG Accountable Executives own the SMS and are responsible for ensuring its design and performance.
src.note: Ownership formally rests with the Accountable Executives, but the manual stresses each teammate OWNS SAFETY.

q: Who is responsible for the overall content and quality of the FOM, and who may modify its policies and procedures?
a: The Managing Director, Standards, Fleet, and Operational Control is responsible for overall content and quality; the Director, Flight Standards, or their designee, has authority to establish and modify policies and procedures.

src.quote: The Managing Director, Standards, Fleet, and Operational Control is responsible for the overall content and quality of this manual.
src.note: Two distinct roles: one owns content and quality, the other holds authority to change policies and procedures.

q: Where can questions about this manual's content or suggested improvements be sent?
a: To flightstandards@alaskaair.com.

src.quote: Questions about the content of this manual or suggested improvements should be sent to flightstandards@alaskaair.com.
src.note: This is the single feedback channel for FOM content questions and improvement suggestions.

q: What is the purpose of airline identifiers such as (AS) and (HA) in the manual?
a: They distinguish differences in policies and procedures between Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

src.quote: Airline identifiers are used to distinguish the differences in policies and procedures for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.
src.note: Placed after a heading when the whole topic is airline-specific, or before content in a paragraph when only that portion applies; a color-filled end box (AS or HA) may be used.

q: Where are terms and definitions used in this manual found?
a: In the Pilot/Controller Glossary of the AIM, the Introduction of the Jeppesen General Airway Manual, and 14 CFR Part 1; unique terms and acronyms are in Chapter 26 Abbreviations and Acronyms.

src.quote: Terms and definitions used within this manual can be found in the Pilot/Controller Glossary of the AIM, the Introduction of the Jeppesen General Airway Manual, and 14 CFR Part 1.
src.note: General definitions live in those three external sources; manual-specific terms and acronyms are consolidated in Chapter 26.

q: What does Green Policy guidance support, and what constraint always overrides it?
a: It supports Flight Crews in making operational decisions aligned with AAG's commitment to fuel efficiency, but safety is always the top priority and fuel-saving measures must never compromise safety.

src.quote: Fuel saving measures must never compromise safety under any circumstances.
src.note: Green guidance is marked with a symbol and targets fleet-wide fuel savings, but never at the expense of safety.

q: Under Compliance with Regulations, what happens in the event of conflicting directives?
a: The more restrictive directive will apply.

src.quote: In the event of conflicting directives, the more restrictive directive will apply.
src.note: Operations must comply with all applicable Laws, Regulations, Operations Specifications, and the CMS; no regulation or policy replaces sound judgment and a commitment to safety.

q: Where can teammates file safety reports?
a: The Virtual Safety Center, safety reporting apps on company-issued mobile devices, Alaska's World Vendor Portal, and the Safety Hotline (on the back of all teammate badges).

src.quote: AAG has provided a non-punitive safety reporting system for all teammates and business partners.
src.note: The system is non-punitive so long as the teammate was not engaged in unacceptable behaviors, and offers four filing channels.

q: What behaviors are defined as 'unacceptable' and therefore outside safety-reporting protection?
a: Illegal activities, intentional disregard for safety/regulations/policies/procedures, drug and alcohol use, workplace violence, reckless conduct and/or willful misconduct, and falsification of records.

src.quote: Unacceptable behaviors are defined as illegal activities, intentional disregard for safety, regulations, policies, or procedures, drug and alcohol use, workplace violence, reckless conduct and/or willful misconduct, and falsification of records.
src.note: These are established in the AAG Code of Conduct and Ethics; filing a report otherwise will not result in discipline.

q: SCENARIO: You are the Captain on the A330 during a line trip. A situation develops that is not covered anywhere in the FOM, and following the nearest published procedure would clearly be unsafe given the conditions. What does the FOM authorize you to do?
a: Exercise your PIC authority to deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety. Per the FOM, it is not possible to develop detailed procedures for all conceivable situations, and as set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557 the PIC has the authority and responsibility to deviate, scoped to what safety requires, using decision-making that serves the intent of providing the highest level of operational safety.

src.quote: As set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557, the PIC has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety.
src.note: Deviation authority is not a blank check; it is bounded by 'to the extent required in the interest of safety,' and the FOM's philosophy supports decisions that serve the intent of the highest level of operational safety when published guidance is inadequate or inappropriate.

q: SCENARIO: On IOE, your check airman points out that two Company manuals give conflicting guidance for the same task, one is more permissive, one is more restrictive. Which do you apply, and what FOM rule governs?
a: Apply the more restrictive guidance. Per FOM 1.1.1, in the event of conflicting manual guidance the more restrictive guidance will apply, and FOM 1.5 repeats the same principle for conflicting directives across the Company Manual System.

src.quote: In the event of conflicting manual guidance, the more restrictive guidance will apply.
src.note: The 'most restrictive wins' rule appears twice, 1.1.1 for conflicting manual guidance and 1.5 for conflicting directives, so conflict always resolves toward the stricter standard.

q: SCENARIO: After a line flight you realize you and the other pilot had a procedural non-compliance, nothing was damaged and no one was hurt, but a step was missed. It feels awkward to write it up. What does the FOM say you should do?
a: File a safety report. The FOM states that reporting close calls and procedural non-compliance is critical because they are early warning signs, and AAG provides a non-punitive safety reporting system. File via the Virtual Safety Center, the safety reporting apps on company-issued devices, Alaska's World Vendor Portal, or the Safety Hotline on the back of your badge; if your division participates in ASAP, you may submit an ASAP report.

src.quote: Reporting close calls and procedural non-compliance is also critical.
src.note: Protection is non-punitive as long as you were not engaged in unacceptable behaviors; close calls and non-compliance are early warning signs that let the Company fix problems before something worse happens.

q: How does the FOM define "operational control" with respect to a flight?
a: The exercise of authority over initiating, conducting, or terminating a flight.

src.quote: Operational control with respect to a flight means the exercise of authority over initiating, conducting, or terminating a flight.
src.note: This is the core definition, repeated verbatim in 2.2.1. Remember the three verbs: initiating, conducting, terminating.

q: Who has the authority for the supervision and control of all Alaska Airlines flights?
a: The 14 CFR Part 119 designated Director of Operations (DO).

src.quote: The 14 CFR Part 119 designated Director of Operations (DO) has the authority for the supervision and control of all Alaska Airlines flights.
src.note: The DO sits at the top of the operational-control structure under Part 119.

q: To whom has the DO delegated the authority to conduct certain operational-control functions?
a: The Flight Operations Duty Officer (FODO).

src.quote: The DO has delegated the authority to conduct certain functions to the Flight Operations Duty Officer (FODO).
src.note: The FODO acts on delegated DO authority for daily oversight of line flying operations.

q: For what three items are the PIC and Aircraft Dispatcher jointly responsible under Joint Responsibility?
a: The preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight.

src.quote: The PIC and Aircraft Dispatcher are jointly responsible for the preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight in compliance with Federal Aviation Regulations
src.note: Both must agree the flight can be accomplished safely; agreement is shown by their signatures on the Dispatch Release.

q: If the flight cannot be completed safely due to hazardous conditions but the PIC believes there is no safer procedure than continuing toward the airport, what does that continuation become?
a: An emergency.

src.quote: unless, in the opinion of the PIC, there is no safer procedure. In that event, continuation toward that airport is an emergency.
src.note: The PIC may not otherwise allow a flight to continue toward a dispatched airport if it cannot be completed safely due to hazardous conditions.

q: How is the PIC's and Dispatcher's agreement that the flight can be accomplished safely indicated?
a: By the signatures of the PIC and Dispatcher on the Dispatch Release.

src.quote: Agreement is indicated by the signatures of the PIC and Dispatcher on the Dispatch Release.
src.note: Both must agree the flight as planned can be accomplished safely and in accordance with 14 CFR and Company policy.

q: When conditions change enroute so the flight cannot be conducted in accordance with the Dispatch Release, who is required to contact whom?
a: The person encountering or learning of the changed conditions must contact the other to institute the necessary amendment to the Dispatch Release.

src.quote: it is required that the person encountering or learning of the changed conditions contact the other to institute the necessary amendment to the Dispatch Release.
src.note: The duty to initiate an amendment falls on whoever learns of the change first, PIC or Dispatcher.

q: What is the scope of the PIC's control and authority over other crewmembers during flight time?
a: Full control and authority in the operation of the aircraft, without limitation, over other crewmembers and their duties during flight time, whether or not they hold valid certificates authorizing those duties.

src.quote: The PIC has full control and authority in the operation of the aircraft, without limitation, over other crewmembers and their duties during flight time, whether or not they hold valid certificates authorizing them to perform the duties of those crewmembers.
src.note: This mirrors 14 CFR 91.3 PIC authority; crewmembers shall comply with the PIC's orders.

q: What must happen if the PIC is not sure that any aspect of flight operations can be safely executed and in compliance with regulations?
a: The operation will be stopped.

src.quote: If the PIC is not sure that any aspect of flight operations can be safely executed and in compliance with regulations, then the operation will be stopped.
src.note: When in doubt about safety or compliance, the default is to stop, not to press on.

q: During a training or evaluation event conducted by a Check Pilot from a pilot seat, who is the designated PIC?
a: The Check Pilot is the designated PIC.

src.quote: Any time a training/evaluation event is being conducted by a Check Pilot from a pilot seat, the Check Pilot is the designated PIC.
src.note: This shifts designated PIC status to the Check Pilot whenever they run the event from a pilot seat.

q: For what period is the PIC's control and authority in effect (Duration of Command)?
a: From the time they report for duty until the termination of the flight.

src.quote: The PIC’s control and authority is in effect from the time they report for duty until the termination of the flight.
src.note: Command authority begins at report-for-duty, not at pushback, and runs through flight termination.

q: What is the sequence of command listed in the Chain of Command?
a: Captain (PIC); International Relief Officer (IRO)/Second in Command (SIC); PIC-qualified First Officer; First Officer; "A" Flight Attendant/FFA; Flight Attendants in descending order.

src.quote: The sequence of command is as follows:
src.note: The list runs Captain, IRO/SIC, PIC-qualified FO, FO, then the A Flight Attendant/FFA and remaining Flight Attendants.

q: On a flight with an augmented Flight Crew, who becomes the acting Captain when the assigned Captain begins their rest period?
a: The IRO becomes the acting Captain.

src.quote: when the assigned Captain begins their rest period, the IRO will become the acting Captain.
src.note: The IRO steps up to acting Captain for the duration of the Captain's rest on an augmented crew.

q: In the Flight Operations Structure, what role does the FODO serve relative to the Director of Operations?
a: The FODO serves as a direct representative of the Director of Operations.

src.quote: The FODO serves as a direct representative of the Director of Operations.
src.note: Operational-control decisions are made under the DO's authority by the Dispatcher, the PIC, and, when required, the FODO.

q: When does the Operational Control Window (OCW) start and end for a normal flight?
a: It starts two and a half hours (D-150) prior to the scheduled departure time and ends when the aircraft is blocked in at the destination airport.

src.quote: OCW starts two and a half hours (D-150) prior to the scheduled departure time and ends when the aircraft is blocked in at the destination airport.
src.note: D-150 means 150 minutes (two and a half hours) before scheduled departure; the window closes at block-in.

q: Which flights get a D-180 Operational Control Window instead of D-150, and where is that list?
a: Flights requiring the Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan 180 minutes prior to scheduled departure, listed in 8.5.2.1: South Korea departures, Amazon Cargo, and (787/A330) Europe departures. All others are D-150.

src.quote: For flights which require the Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan to be produced 180 minutes prior to scheduled departure, the OCW starts three hours (D-180), see 8.5.2.1 – Dispatch Release – Preparation.
src.note: South Korea, Amazon Cargo and (787/A330) Europe departures get a three-hour (D-180) window versus the standard D-150 (two and a half hours). The Europe line is new in Rev 125 and applies to the A330.

q: Within the OCW, a decision to cancel or modify a flight is an operational control action requiring coordination and endorsement from whom, and who is ultimately responsible?
a: It requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC; the Director of Operations is ultimately responsible.

src.quote: any decision to cancel or modify the flight is an operational control action which requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC.
src.note: The FODO and Pilot Crew Scheduling provide guidance when required, but the DO is ultimately responsible.

q: May a Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate act as PIC or IRO?
a: No. A Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO.

src.quote: A Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO.
src.note: The IRO is SIC of the aircraft and assumes command if the Captain is incapacitated, so a restricted ATP is disqualifying for that seat.

q: What phases of flight constitute a Sterile Flight Deck (critical phases of flight)?
a: Ground operations involving pushback, towing, taxi, takeoff, and landing; and all other flight operations conducted below 10,000 ft MSL, except cruise flight.

src.quote: All other flight operations conducted below 10,000 ft MSL, except cruise flight.
src.note: The deck is not considered sterile during lengthy ground holds when the parking brake is set.

q: What bank angle and nose-up pitch attitude should normal flying not require to be exceeded?
a: Bank angles greater than 30 degrees or pitch attitude greater than 20 degrees nose up.

src.ref: FOM 2.3.14, Style of Flying/Bank and Pitch Angles
src.quote: Normal flying should not require bank angles greater than 30° or airspeeds higher than the normal limit speed or pitch attitude greater than 20° nose up.
src.note: Aircraft may exceed 20 nose up under certain flight conditions or departure/climb profiles.

q: Check-airman scenario: airborne, an event requires the PIC to deviate from a Company procedure and from an ATC clearance to keep the aircraft safe. What authority lets the PIC do this on their own?
a: The PIC may unilaterally exercise emergency authority.

src.quote: May unilaterally exercise emergency authority.
src.note: Listed among the PIC's responsibilities in the job description; echoes 14 CFR 91.3 emergency authority. "Unilaterally" means no prior coordination is required to act.

q: Check-airman scenario: enroute, the PIC is unsure whether a reroute still allows the flight to be conducted per the Dispatch Release. Per the FOM, who is the PIC's contact and the primary source of flight-status information?
a: The Dispatcher.

src.quote: When the PIC has an issue related to operational control of a flight, the PIC should contact the Dispatcher. The Dispatcher is the primary source of information related to the status of a flight
src.note: Under joint responsibility the Dispatcher, not crew scheduling or the gate, is the PIC's operational-control contact for delay, reroute, or cancellation.

q: Check-airman scenario: on an augmented crew, the Captain becomes incapacitated during cruise. Per the chain of command, who assumes command?
a: The IRO assumes command, performs the Captain's duties, and assumes the Captain's responsibilities.

src.quote: If the Captain becomes incapacitated, the IRO will assume command, perform the Captain’s duties, and assume the Captain’s responsibilities.
src.note: This is why a Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO, the IRO can inherit command.

q: Check-airman scenario: inside the Operational Control Window, the NOC business group wants to cancel your flight for commercial reasons. What does the FOM require, and who is ultimately responsible?
a: Inside the OCW, canceling or modifying is an operational control action requiring coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC; the Director of Operations is ultimately responsible.

src.quote: Within the OCW, any decision to cancel or modify the flight is an operational control action which requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC.
src.note: Contrast 2.2.2.2: before the OCW the same decision is a business decision that does not require operational-control endorsement.

q: What is the minimum EFB battery charge to begin a flight duty day or training event, and what is the minimum for a departure?
a: 80% to begin a flight duty day or training event, unless the pilot carries an external backup battery of sufficient capacity and charge. 20% minimum for a departure.

src.quote: To begin a flight duty day or training event, the minimum EFB battery charge status required is 80%, unless the pilot carries an external backup battery of sufficient capacity and charge. • Before each flight: minimum EFB battery charge for a departure is 20%.
src.note: New in Rev 124.2. Two numbers: 80% to show up, 20% to depart.

q: How long before a flight must a person requesting jumpseat access (or issued a jumpseat boarding pass) not consume alcohol?
a: Within 10 hours of the flight. If issued a jumpseat boarding pass, alcohol shall not be consumed on board.

src.quote: Any individual requesting jumpseat access or issued a jumpseat boarding pass (even if occupying a seat in the cabin) shall not consume alcohol within 10 hours of the flight. If issued a jumpseat boarding pass, alcohol shall not be consumed on board.
src.note: Rev 125 wording. Also: occupants must not consume alcohol in the cabin before using the crew rest facility, and deadheading crewmembers may not consume alcohol in or out of uniform.

q: May a working Flight Crewmember bring a dependent under 13 as a non-rev on their own operating flight?
a: Only if another adult accompanies the dependent. Family members must adhere to all non-rev travel rules.

src.ref: FOM 2.6.15, Traveling with Family While on Duty
src.quote: Working crewmembers may have family non-rev on the same operating flight. Family members must adhere to all non-rev travel rules. Working Flight Crews may not bring dependents under the age of 13 on flights unless another adult accompanies the dependent.
src.note: New section in Rev 125.

q: On which operations is the uniform blazer required?
a: Blazers are required on international widebody passenger operations.

src.quote: Blazers are required on international widebody passenger operations.
src.note: Rev 125 uniform guidance. The blazer carries metal wings and sleeve rating stripes reflecting current awarded status regardless of seat occupied.

q: For AS operations, what is the maximum number of Flight Crewmembers on a pairing who may have less than 150 hours line operating flight time in type and crew position? What is the HA figure?
a: Only one Flight Crewmember (CA, F/O, IRO) may have less than (AS) 150 hours line operating flight time at the Company (including OE) in type and crew position (seat). The HA figure is 100 hours in type.

src.quote: For all operations, only one Flight Crewmember (CA, F/O, IRO) may have less than: • (AS) 150 hours line operating flight time at the Company (including Operating Experience, “OE”) in type and crew position (seat). • (HA) 100 hours line operating flight time at the Company (including Operating Experience, “OE”) in type.
src.note: Applies to all operations under 14 CFR 121.438. The HA equivalent threshold is 100 hours line operating flight time in type.

q: How many hours in type must a qualified Check Pilot have to be exempt from the crew pairing requirement while performing Check Pilot duties?
a: At least 75 hours in type.

src.quote: A qualified Check Pilot with at least 75 hours in type is not subject to this pairing requirement while performing Check Pilot duties.
src.note: The exemption applies only while the Check Pilot is actually performing Check Pilot duties.

q: First Officers with less than how many hours in aircraft type at Alaska Airlines may not make takeoffs or landings at special airports?
a: First Officers with less than 100 hours in aircraft type at Alaska Airlines shall not make takeoffs or landings at special airports.

src.quote: First Officers with less than 100 hours in aircraft type at Alaska Airlines shall not make takeoffs or landings at special airports
src.note: FAA Special Airports are marked "Airport Qualification" on the Jeppesen 19-XX chart; "Airport Familiarization" charts carry no qualification/currency requirement.

q: To satisfy PIC Special Airport currency by making a takeoff or landing to that airport, what ceiling and visibility conditions must exist?
a: The ceiling must be at least 1000 ft above the lowest MEA or MOCA, or initial approach altitude prescribed for the instrument approach for that airport, and visibility at least 3 miles.

src.quote: Make a takeoff or landing to that airport if the ceiling at that airport is at least 1000 ft above the lowest MEA or MOCA, or initial approach altitude prescribed for the instrument approach for that airport and the visibility is at least 3 miles.
src.note: Alternatively, currency may be re-established within the preceding 12 calendar months by an aircraft/level-D sim entry or by reviewing the FAA-accepted Jeppesen FD Pro airport pictorials.

q: How often must a pilot accomplish a NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember to maintain North Atlantic High-Level Airspace currency on the A330?
a: At least one NAT HLA segment every 24 months.

src.ref: FOM 3.3.4, North Atlantic High-Level Airspace (NAT HLA) Qualification (787/A330)
src.quote: Pilots are required to accomplish at least one NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember every 24 months.
src.note: NAT HLA qualification applies to qualified PICs and SICs; see the applicable FOTM for the requirements to re-establish currency once it lapses.

q: For Consolidation, how many hours of line operating flight time must Captains and First Officers acquire, and within what period of their Qual LOE in type?
a: 100 hours of line operating flight time at Alaska Airlines within 120 days of their Qual LOE in type (flight time includes OE).

src.quote: Captains and First Officers must acquire 100 hours of line operating flight time at Alaska Airlines within 120 days of their Qual LOE in type.
src.note: Prior consolidation in type as PIC or SIC satisfies the requirement for all seats in that aircraft type. Resting time on augmented flights cannot be counted toward consolidation.

q: For consolidation on augmented flights, how much of the flight segment's total hours is subtracted for double augment versus single augment?
a: 50% is subtracted for double augment and 33% for single augment.

src.quote: For augmented crews, the total hours of the flight segment will be subtracted as follows: • 50% for double augment • 33% for single augment
src.note: Time spent resting, while not seated at the controls, cannot count toward OE or consolidation requirements.

q: To qualify for Captain Upgrade, how many hours SIC at the Company must a pilot have?
a: 1000 hours SIC at the Company, or the pilot must meet the requirements listed in 14 CFR 121.436.

src.quote: To qualify for Captain Upgrade, a pilot must have 1000 hours SIC at the Company or meet the requirements listed in 14 CFR 121.436.
src.note: The upgrade requirement is governed by 14 CFR 121.436.

q: Under the Initial First Officer takeoff/landing restrictions, at what crosswind component must the Captain make all takeoffs and landings (unless the FO is paired with a Check Pilot)?
a: When the crosswind component is greater than 15 kts (for a First Officer with less than 100 hours in aircraft type).

src.ref: FOM 3.6, Initial First Officer Restrictions – Takeoff and Landing
src.quote: The crosswind component is greater than 15 kts
src.note: The Captain must also make all takeoffs and landings at special airports, on contaminated runways, when braking action is less than GOOD, when windshear is reported nearby, or when visibility is at or below 3/4 sm or RVR at or below 4000.

q: A High Minimums Captain is any Captain with less than how many hours as PIC in type at the Company?
a: Less than 100 hours as a PIC in type at the Company.

src.quote: High minimums apply to any Captain who has less than 100 hours as a PIC in type at the Company.
src.note: The Captain must advise Dispatch of high minimums status prior to each flight segment when weather is reported or forecast below 1000 ft ceiling and 3 miles visibility at or near time of landing.

q: For military charter operations, what combined minimum total flight hours in the aircraft type must the Captain and First Officer have?
a: A combined minimum of 250 total flight hours in the aircraft type (except for aircraft new to the Company).

src.ref: FOM 3.8, High Minimums Crewmembers – Military Charters
src.quote: The Captain and First Officer must have a combined minimum of 250 total flight hours in the aircraft type except for aircraft new to the Company, to operate any military charter operations.
src.note: This requirement stems from 32 CFR 861 governing military charter operations.

q: How many hours as PIC in type at the Company must a Captain have to perform CAT III operations, and is it reducible?
a: A minimum of 100 hours as PIC in type at the Company, and it is not reducible.

src.ref: FOM 3.15, Category III Operations – Captain Hours Required
src.quote: Captain must have minimum of 100 hours as PIC in type at the Company (not reducible) to perform CAT III operations.
src.note: During Captain OE, CAT III is not authorized for the qualifying Captain unless they had previously met this hours requirement.

q: For SA CAT I / CAT II operations under Exemption 5549, how many hours as a pilot in a turbojet aircraft must the Captain have?
a: A minimum of 300 hours as a pilot (PIC or SIC) in a turbojet aircraft.

src.ref: FOM 3.16.2, SA CAT I/CAT II Operations at Destination or Alternate
src.quote: The Captain has a minimum of 300 hours as a pilot (PIC or SIC) in a turbojet aircraft
src.note: For AS the Captain must also comply with the SA CAT I/II Approach Briefing Card.

q: During Captain/First Officer OE takeoffs, at what RVR must the left seat occupant conduct all takeoffs?
a: The left seat occupant will conduct all takeoffs when the RVR is 1600 ft or less.

src.quote: The left seat occupant will conduct all takeoffs when the RVR is 1600 ft or less.
src.note: During OE the Check Pilot is the Company-designated PIC and must occupy a pilot seat.

q: What is the Takeoff and Landing Currency requirement, including the currency interval and any limit on Autolands?
a: At least 3 takeoffs and landings within 90 days, in the specific aircraft type or an AS-approved simulator, in either seat; only one of the required landings may be an Autoland. Documented by ACARS entry.

src.ref: FOM 3.19, Operational Currency and Training Requirements
src.quote: Only one of the required landings may be an Autoland.
src.note: The currency interval is 90 days; credit for an Autoland landing may go to both the Captain and First Officer.

q: Under Exemption 5549, if the crosswind component exceeds 15 kts combined with a braking action report of less than 'good,' what minimum visibility is required?
a: Visibility must be at least 4000 RVR (3/4 mile visibility).

src.ref: FOM 3.16.1, CAT I Precision Approach at Destination or Alternate
src.quote: If the crosswind component exceeds 15 kts combined with a braking action report of less than “good,” visibility must be at least 4000 RVR (3/4 mile visibility).
src.note: For AS the approach is flown by the Captain with the autopilot coupled to the approach to DH or missed approach.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are an A330 First Officer and monthly bid closure is tomorrow. A check airman notices your last takeoff and landing was 91 days ago, so your Takeoff and Landing Currency has lapsed. Under FOM 3.19, what happens to next month's bid and how do you correct the deficiency?
a: Because the currency requirement was not maintained, the following month's bid will not be honored and you will be removed from flight duty and payroll until the deficiency is corrected. Currency deficiencies are corrected by submission of appropriate Training Certification Forms, simulator requalification, or supervised line flying.

src.ref: FOM 3.19, Operational Currency and Training Requirements
src.quote: (AS) Failure to initially accomplish and/or maintain currency requirements will result in the following month’s bid not being honored and will result in removal from flight duty and payroll until any deficiencies are corrected.
src.note: Operational currency and training requirements must be accomplished prior to monthly bid closure; Takeoff and Landing Currency is documented by ACARS entry.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A check airman reviews your last 90 days and finds 3 takeoffs and landings in the A330, but 2 of the 3 landings were Autolands. Are you legally current for Takeoff and Landing Currency under FOM 3.19, and why or why not?
a: No. Only one of the three required landings may be an Autoland, so at least two must be hand-flown landings. With two Autolands you are one manual landing short and are not current.

src.ref: FOM 3.19, Operational Currency and Training Requirements
src.quote: Only one of the required landings may be an Autoland.
src.note: Landings may be in the specific aircraft type or an AS-approved simulator, in either seat; credit for an Autoland landing may go to both the Captain and First Officer.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Scheduling wants to assign you as a required Flight Crewmember on an A330 segment through North Atlantic High-Level Airspace, but your last NAT HLA segment was 25 months ago. Under FOM 3.3.4, are you current for NAT HLA, and what governs re-establishing it?
a: No. NAT HLA currency requires accomplishing at least one NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember every 24 months; at 25 months your currency has lapsed. Re-establishing currency is governed by the Non-737 FOTM.

src.ref: FOM 3.3.4, North Atlantic High-Level Airspace (NAT HLA) Qualification (787/A330)
src.quote: Pilots are required to accomplish at least one NAT HLA segment as a required Flight Crewmember every 24 months.
src.note: NAT HLA qualification applies to qualified PICs and SICs on the 787 and A330; see the Non-737 FOTM for the requirements to re-establish currency once it lapses.

q: How far in advance of scheduled departure must a pilot check in with Pilot Crew Scheduling for the originating flight of a pairing, and what is the deadheading check-in time?
a: One hour prior to scheduled departure, or 45 minutes prior for deadheading.

src.quote: Pilots shall check in one hour prior (45 minutes for deadheading) to the scheduled departure of the originating flight of a pairing.
src.note: Missing the one-hour check-in can trigger assignment of a reserve pilot and a possible 'No Show' pending Base Chief Pilot review.

q: A pilot may voluntarily check in earlier than one hour before departure, but no earlier than what limit?
a: No earlier than four hours prior to the scheduled departure.

src.quote: a pilot may voluntarily check-in prior to one hour, but in no case earlier than four hours prior to the scheduled departure.
src.note: Early check-in is at the individual pilot's discretion but is bounded at four hours before scheduled departure.

q: What is the minimum pilot crew for a flight, and how are the two positions designated?
a: Two pilots: one designated as Pilot-In-Command and one as Second-In-Command.

src.quote: The minimum pilot crew is two pilots; one pilot designated as Pilot-In-Command and one as Second-In-Command.
src.note: Each pilot is designated no more than one Flight Crew function per flight segment.

q: Under Part 117 Table A (unaugmented), what maximum flight time applies for a report time of 0500-1959 versus 0000-0459 or 2000-2359?
a: 9 hours for a report time of 0500-1959; 8 hours for report times of 0000-0459 or 2000-2359.

src.quote: the flight time limits in Table A of Part 117 (unaugmented operations) restrict a Flight Crewmember’s time on task (flight time) to either 8 or 9 hours.
src.note: Table A is entered using the report time at local domicile or the acclimated local time in theater; 0500-1959 gives 9 hours, the two night bands give 8.

q: For augmented operations, the Part 117 flight time limits restrict time on task to what values for a 3-pilot crew versus a 4-pilot crew?
a: 13 hours for a 3-pilot crew and 17 hours for a 4-pilot crew.

src.quote: Flight time limits (augmented operations) restrict a Flight Crewmember’s time on task (flight time) to either 13 hours (3-pilot crew) or 17 hours (4-pilot crew).
src.note: These are flight-time (time-on-task) limits, distinct from the Flight Duty Period limits in Tables B and C.

q: What are the cumulative flight time limitations a Flight Crewmember may not exceed under Part 117?
a: 100 hours in any 672 consecutive hours, or 1000 hours in any 365 consecutive calendar-day period.

src.quote: A Flight Crewmember’s cumulative FTL shall not exceed: • 100 hours in any 672 consecutive hours, or • 1000 hours in any 365 consecutive calendar-day period.
src.note: Cumulative FTL uses rolling windows of 672 consecutive hours and 365 consecutive calendar days and includes all Part 91 and 121 flying.

q: What are the cumulative Flight Duty Period (FDP) limits under Part 117?
a: 60 FDP hours in any 168 consecutive hours, or 190 FDP hours in any 672 consecutive hours.

src.quote: • 60 FDP hours in any 168 consecutive hours, or • 190 FDP hours in any 672 consecutive hours.
src.note: A post-takeoff FDP extension may exceed these cumulative limits only to the extent necessary to complete the flight; it expires once the aircraft lands.

q: What is the minimum rest period Part 117 prescribes before a RAP or between FDPs, and what sleep opportunity must it provide?
a: 10 consecutive hours measured from release from duty, providing a minimum of 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity.

src.quote: the minimum rest period (prior to beginning a Reserve Availability Period (RAP) or between FDPs) as 10 consecutive hours measured from the time the Flight Crewmember is released from duty. This 10-hour rest period must provide the Flight Crewmember with a minimum of 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity.
src.note: If the pilot determines the rest will not provide 10 hours or the 8 uninterrupted sleep hours, they must notify Pilot Crew Scheduling.

q: What is the maximum FDP extension permitted under 14 CFR 117.19, and what is the prior-extension gate?
a: Up to 2 hours, provided neither Flight Crewmember has had an extension greater than 30 minutes since their last period of 30 consecutive hours free from all duty.

src.quote: Flight Duty Period (FDP) extensions of up to 2 hours are permitted provided:
src.note: Other conditions: the extension addresses unforeseen operational circumstances, CBA/PWA limits are not exceeded, and the PIC and certificate holder agree on the length.

q: How does a Flight Crewmember become acclimated to a new theater under Part 117?
a: By receiving 36 consecutive hours of rest in the new theater, or by having been in the new theater for 72 hours.

src.quote: A Flight Crewmember operating in a new theater that has received 36 consecutive hours of rest, or who has been in a new theater for 72 hours, is considered to be acclimated to that new theater.
src.note: If a crewmember transitions theaters and is not acclimated, the Table B or Table C maximum FDP limit must be reduced by 30 minutes.

q: How does Part 117 define a 'theater' for acclimation purposes?
a: A geographical area where the FDP departure and arrival points differ by no more than 60 degrees of longitude.

src.quote: Theater means a geographical area in which the distance between the Flight Crewmember’s flight duty period departure point and arrival point differs by no more than 60 degrees of longitude.
src.note: The same 60-degree-longitude threshold drives theater-change compensatory rest in 4.3.2.11.

q: What is the minimum recline requirement that defines a Class 3 rest facility?
a: A seat in an aircraft cabin or Flight Deck that reclines at least 40 degrees and provides leg and foot support.

src.quote: Class 3 rest facility means a seat in an aircraft cabin or Flight Deck that reclines at least 40 degrees and provides leg and foot support.
src.note: Class 1 (flat bunk, isolated) yields the longest FDP limit; Class 3 provides the least quality and the shortest augmented FDP limit.

q: How many consecutive nighttime FDPs infringing on the WOCL are Flight Crewmembers limited to, and what are the WOCL hours?
a: A maximum of three consecutive nighttime FDPs scheduled to infringe on the WOCL, which is 0200-0559.

src.quote: Flight Crewmembers are limited to a maximum of three consecutive nighttime FDPs that are scheduled to infringe on WOCL (0200-0559).
src.note: This applies whenever an FDP infringes on any part of the crewmember's Window of Circadian Low.

q: For a short-call reserve pilot, what is the maximum length of a Reserve Availability Period (RAP)?
a: The RAP may not exceed 14 hours.

src.quote: The Flight Crewmember’s RAP may not exceed 14 hours.
src.note: The combined RAP plus FDP may not exceed the lesser of the applicable Table B FDP limit plus 4 hours, or 16 hours, measured from the start of the RAP.

q: Within what time must a Fatigue Report be submitted for a fatigue call in order for pay protection to be considered?
a: Within 3 days of the fatigue event, in a timely manner.

src.quote: A Fatigue Report must be submitted for a fatigue call in a timely manner (within 3 days of the fatigue event) in order for pay protection to be considered.
src.note: If the FRP finds extenuating circumstances precluded timely submission, it may still accept the report for a pay evaluation.

q: By no later than what time prior to departure should the Captain be on board the aircraft?
a: On board prior to passenger boarding if possible, but no later than 25 minutes prior to departure.

src.quote: Captain – Be on board prior to passenger boarding, if possible, but no later than 25 minutes prior to departure.
src.note: The First Officer arrives at the aircraft at least 45 minutes prior for preflight and should be on board 20 minutes prior to departure.

q: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're the PIC on a long Pacific pairing. An unforeseen gate hold has pushed you toward your Flight Duty Period limit and Pilot Crew Scheduling asks for an extension so you can complete the flight. What is the maximum FDP extension, and what prior-extension condition must be satisfied before you can accept it?
a: Up to 2 hours, provided neither Flight Crewmember has experienced an extension greater than 30 minutes since their last period of 30 consecutive hours free from all duty (and the extension addresses unforeseen operational circumstances, CBA/PWA limits are not exceeded, and the PIC and certificate holder agree on the length).

src.quote: Flight Duty Period (FDP) extensions of up to 2 hours are permitted provided: • Extension is required to address unforeseen operational circumstances. • Neither Flight Crewmember has experienced an extension greater than 30 minutes since the crewmember’s last period of 30 consecutive hours free from all duty.
src.note: Pilot Crew Scheduling and/or the Flight Operations Duty Officer are authorized to act on behalf of the certificate holder in agreeing upon the length of the extension.

q: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: After a red-eye Pacific crossing you determine you are too fatigued to safely fly the next leg. What action does the FOM require of you to be removed from the assignment, and what is the disciplinary consequence of removing yourself for fatigue on the Alaska side?
a: You must contact and advise Pilot Crew Scheduling in order to be removed from the flight assignment (and should complete a Fatigue Report). Removal from assignments for flight time due to fatigue will not be cause for disciplinary action.

src.quote: If a Flight Crewmember feels they are too fatigued to fly, the Flight Crewmember shall contact and advise Pilot Crew Scheduling in order to be removed from the flight assignment. A Fatigue Report should be completed to identify and address any systemic conditions that caused the fatigue (see 7.2.2 – Reporting Program). (AS) Removal from assignments for flight time due to fatigue will not be cause for disciplinary action, and will be accomplished as follows:
src.note: To be considered for pay protection, the Fatigue Report must be submitted within 3 days of the event (FOM 4.3.1.4).

q: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: On a long Pacific pairing your scheduled outstation layover looks like it will not give you a full 10 hours of rest or the 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. What does Part 117 prescribe for minimum rest, and what is your obligation when you spot the shortfall?
a: Minimum rest is 10 consecutive hours measured from release from duty, and that period must provide at least 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. If you determine your scheduled rest will not provide the 10 hours or the 8 uninterrupted sleep hours, you must notify Pilot Crew Scheduling.

src.quote: Part 117 prescribes the minimum rest period (prior to beginning a Reserve Availability Period (RAP) or between FDPs) as 10 consecutive hours measured from the time the Flight Crewmember is released from duty. This 10-hour rest period must provide the Flight Crewmember with a minimum of 8 uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity.
src.note: The assignment must be scheduled in advance so the crewmember can plan to maximize sleep opportunity within the rest period.

q: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're airborne on a long over-water leg when an unforeseen circumstance means finishing the flight will push you past your cumulative FDP limits. Is exceeding those cumulative limits permitted, and what is the catch?
a: Yes. Under 14 CFR 117.19 a post-takeoff FDP extension allows a Flight Crewmember to exceed the cumulative FDP limits, but only to the extent necessary to complete that flight, and the extension expires once the aircraft lands.

src.quote: Under 14 CFR 117.19, a post-takeoff FDP extension allows a Flight Crewmember to exceed the cumulative FDP limits. However, a post-takeoff FDP extension is limited in that it expires once the aircraft lands. Once the flight on which the post-takeoff extension was used has been completed, the Flight Crewmember would again be bound by the cumulative FDP limitations.
src.note: Cumulative FDP limits are 60 hours in any 168 consecutive hours and 190 hours in any 672 consecutive hours.

q: On the A330, what takeoff and landing operations are authorized on a narrow runway, and how is a narrow runway defined?
a: None. On the A330 (as on the 717, 787 and A321), takeoff and landing are not authorized on any narrow runway. A narrow runway is one whose nominal paved width is less than 100 ft (30 m).

src.quote: (717/787/A321/A330) Takeoff and landing are not authorized on any narrow runway.
src.note: The 100 ft / 30 m threshold defines a narrow runway; only the 737 has narrow-runway authorization, with restrictions.

q: When must the cabin doors be armed relative to aircraft movement?
a: Doors shall be armed for any surface movement, including all pushbacks, taxi, and towing. Pilots must give Flight Attendants adequate time and notice to secure the cabin for movement.

src.ref: FOM 5.1.7, Door Arming with Passengers on Board
src.quote: Doors shall be armed for any surface movement, including all pushbacks, taxi, and towing
src.note: Applies to every ground movement with passengers aboard, not just pushback.

q: How many start attempts constitute a successful APU start, and when is the APU considered to have failed to start?
a: The APU is considered to have started successfully on any one of three start attempts. It is considered to have failed to start after three consecutive start attempt failures, or when fleet-specific procedures preclude subsequent attempts.

src.quote: an APU is considered to have started successfully on any one of three start attempts
src.note: Three consecutive failures equals a failed start and drives a required Maintenance Logbook entry.

q: During which phases of flight may the crew rest facility not be occupied?
a: It must not be occupied from pushback to 10,000 ft AFE, and from 45 minutes prior to landing to aircraft block-in.

src.quote: The crew rest facility must not be occupied from pushback to 10,000 ft AFE and from 45 minutes prior to landing to aircraft block-in
src.note: Brackets the rest facility to the cruise/enroute window. On the A330 the facility is the Lower Deck Module Crew Rest unit (LDMCR); see 5.1.23.8.

q: Under what braking-action report is taxi prohibited?
a: Taxi operations are prohibited when braking action is reported as NIL by the airport or other aircraft.

src.quote: Taxi operations are prohibited when braking action is reported as NIL by airport or other aircraft
src.note: A NIL braking action report is an absolute bar to taxi.

q: For which taxi clearances is dual acknowledgment between both pilots required?
a: Runway Crossing, Hold Short, Line Up and Wait, Cleared for Takeoff, and Cleared to Land.

src.quote: Dual acknowledgment should be used for all taxi instructions between both pilots and is required for the following clearances
src.note: The listed five clearances require the transmitting pilot's readback plus a verbal confirmation from the other pilot.

q: Who must taxi the aircraft during low visibility operations?
a: The Captain must taxi the aircraft during low visibility operations. Restricted visibility includes any time the RVR is less than 1200.

src.quote: During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft
src.note: Restricted visibility includes dense fog, heavy precipitation, or any time RVR is less than 1200; checklists are done stopped with the parking brake set.

q: What are the standard takeoff minimums for an aircraft with two engines or less?
a: 1 sm visibility or RVR 5000.

src.quote: Defined as 1 sm visibility or RVR 5000 for aircraft having 2 engines or less
src.note: The A330, having two engines, uses this standard; when published minimums are higher and no special procedure exists, takeoff below published minimums is prohibited.

q: What is the maximum takeoff-alternate distance for the A330?

src.note: Per-fleet table in 5.4.2: A321 360 nm, A330 370 nm, 717 320 nm, 737 350 nm, 787 393 nm. Takeoff-alternate weather must meet destination-alternate requirements.

q: At what visibility must the Captain make the takeoff?
a: Any time the visibility is less than or equal to 1/4 sm or 1600 RVR, the Captain will make the takeoff.

src.quote: the visibility is less than or equal to 1/4 sm or 1600 RVR, the Captain will make the takeoff
src.note: The same 1600 RVR / 1/4 sm threshold appears in the lower-than-standard takeoff table as the Captain-required trigger.

q: On the A330, above what speed does a rejected takeoff require a return to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry regardless of the reason?
a: Above 100 kts (Airbus). An RTO initiated at greater than 100 kts requires that the flight return to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry be made regardless of the reason for the RTO.

src.quote: An RTO initiated at greater than (Airbus) 100 kts/(Boeing) 80 kts requires that the flight returns to the gate and a Maintenance Logbook entry be made regardless of the reason for the RTO.
src.note: At or below the Airbus 100 kt threshold for correctable issues, no gate return is required, but brake temperature limits must still be considered and a Maintenance Logbook entry may be required. New speed-based rule in Rev 125.

q: At what minimum height is an initial turn after takeoff normally commenced when no turn point is procedurally defined, and what turn is exempt?
a: Normally at a minimum of 400 ft AFE, to comply with TERPS ODP criteria. A required course or heading change of less than 15 degrees initially is a non-maneuvering turn and may be commenced below 400 ft.

src.quote: an initial turn after takeoff is normally commenced at a minimum of 400 ft AFE
src.note: Applies to departure procedures lacking a defined turn point; a fleet manual or DP-specified altitude overrides the 400 ft default.

q: Within what tolerance must the two primary altimeters agree during RVSM operations, and how often are crosschecks made?
a: The two primary altimeters should agree within 200 ft (or a lesser value if specified in the FH/FCOM). Crosschecks between the primary altimeters and the standby are made at intervals of approximately one hour.

src.ref: FOM 5.5.6.5, Enroute RVSM Altitude Monitoring Requirements
src.quote: The two primary altimeters should agree within 200 ft
src.note: RVSM airspace is FL290 to FL410 inclusive with 1000 ft vertical separation; at level-off all altimeters are set to 29.92, and use of the standby as a primary is prohibited.

q: What assigned-altitude deviation requires a Flight Crew safety report, and within what time?
a: An assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft or more (also an altimeter system error of 245 ft or more, or a total vertical error of 300 ft or more) requires a safety report within 24 hours. The Company must separately report altitude-keeping errors to the FAA within 72 hours.

src.quote: Assigned altitude deviation of 300 ft or more
src.note: 24-hour crew safety report thresholds are 300 ft assigned deviation, 245 ft altimeter system error, and 300 ft total vertical error; Company FAA reporting is within 72 hours.

q: If a pilot leaves their duty station above FL410, what is required of the remaining crewmember?
a: The remaining crewmember must put on and use their oxygen mask before the other pilot leaves the seat and continue using it until the other crewmember has returned.

src.quote: above FL410, the remaining crewmember must put on and utilize their oxygen mask
src.note: The trigger is the aircraft being above FL410 while one pilot is away from the controls.

q: Is the A330 approved for RNP-4 enroute operations?
a: Yes. All Company aircraft are approved for RNP-4 operations, with the exception of the 717, which is limited to RNP-10.

src.quote: All Company aircraft are approved for RNP-4 operations, with the exception of the 717, which is limited to RNP-10.
src.note: RNP-4 is the enroute oceanic/remote navigation capability the A330 carries.

q: On what maximum airspeed is holding pattern protection based?
a: A maximum of 280 KIAS / Mach 0.8, whichever is lower. Standard holding patterns are right-hand turns, and a speed reduction is begun no earlier than three minutes prior to reaching the fix.

src.quote: Holding pattern protection is based on a maximum of 280 KIAS/Mach 0.8, whichever is lower
src.note: US holding max airspeeds by altitude are 200 KIAS at/below 6000, 230 KIAS above 6000 through 14,000, and 265 KIAS above 14,000; holding fuel is calculated every 15 minutes.

q: By what height must the A330 normally be aligned with the runway for an approach to be stabilized?
a: Normally the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE. Approaches that include a 300 ft AFE runway alignment exception are indicated in the relevant airport 10-7.

src.quote: the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE
src.note: An approach is stabilized only if all criteria are met; either crewmember may call a no-fault go-around, and do not land from an unstable approach.

q: What are the circling approach minimums?
a: 1000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility, or the charted circling minimums, whichever is greater.

src.quote: Circling minimums are 1000 ft and 3 sm visibility or charted circling minimums whichever is greater
src.note: After reaching MDA the PF keeps an identifiable portion of the runway environment in sight and maintains MDA until in a position to descend to land.

q: With only the approach lighting system in sight, below what height is descent not allowed, and what would then permit continuing?
a: With only the approach lights in sight, a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight.

src.quote: a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight
src.note: One of the 14 CFR 91.175 visual references must be distinctly visible to continue below DH/MDA; the approach light system alone is limited to 100 ft above TDZE without the red bars.

q: Within what limits must touchdown be planned, and what is the earliest allowable touchdown point from the threshold?
a: Touchdown shall be planned within the first 3000 ft beyond the threshold, the first third of the runway, or (AS) the Latest Touchdown Point, whichever is less. The earliest planned touchdown point shall never be less than 500 ft from the runway threshold.

src.quote: Touchdown shall be planned within the first 3000 ft beyond the threshold, the first third of the runway
src.note: A safety report is required for any touchdown less than 500 ft from the threshold or beyond the applicable distance policy.

q: What are the LAHSO weather minimums, and how do they change with a PAPI or VASI installed and operational?
a: Ceiling no less than 1500 ft and visibility no less than 5 sm. If a PAPI or VASI is installed and operational, conditions may be lowered to a ceiling no less than 1000 ft and visibility no less than 3 sm. LAHSO is prohibited on wet runways, and the tailwind on the hold short runway shall be calm (less than 3 kts).

src.quote: – A ceiling of no less than 1500 ft. – A visibility of no less than 5 sm. – LAHSO weather minima may be lowered to a ceiling of no less than 1000 ft and a visibility of no less than 3 sm where a Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI) or Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI) is installed and operational.
src.note: LAHSO criteria were rewritten in Rev 125: prohibited on wet runways, not authorized to a runway without visual or electronic vertical guidance, not authorized if windshear has been reported.

q: SCENARIO (check airman): You are the PM on an A330 visual to a wet runway. At 400 ft AFE the aircraft is fast and still drifting back toward centerline, not yet aligned. The PF says he will have it by the numbers. By 300 ft AFE it is still not aligned and airspeed is above target. What is the required action and who may take it?
a: The approach is unstable. Normally the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE; it is not aligned by 500 ft, so the stabilized-approach gate is busted. Do not land from an unstable approach. Either crewmember may call for a go-around under the no-fault go-around policy, so the PM calls and the crew goes around.

src.quote: An approach is stabilized only if all criteria are met. Normally, the aircraft must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE. Approaches which include a 300 ft AFE runway alignment exception are indicated in the relevant airport 10-7.
src.note: 500 ft AFE runway alignment is the gate (300 ft AFE only where an exception is published in the 10-7); an unaligned, fast approach past the gate requires a go-around.

q: SCENARIO (check airman): On an ILS in fog you reach DH with only the approach lighting system in sight, no red side row or terminating bars, and no other listed visual reference. The PF continues descending below 100 ft looking for the runway. What is the correct action?
a: This is a violation. With only the approach lighting system in sight, a descent below 100 ft is not allowed unless the red side row bars or the red terminating bars are in sight. With no other 14 CFR 91.175 visual reference distinctly visible, a missed approach must be immediately executed when operating below the DH/MDA. The PF must go around, not continue.

src.quote: A missed approach must be immediately executed if any of the 14 CFR 91.175 requirements are not met when operating below the DH/MDA.
src.note: The approach light system alone permits descent only to 100 ft above TDZE; below that the red side row bars or red terminating bars, or another listed reference, must be distinctly visible or a missed approach is mandatory.

q: SCENARIO (check airman): Level at FL360 in RVSM airspace, you lose one primary altimeter and the autopilot altitude-control system flags a fault, so required RVSM equipment is no longer operating normally. Can you reset and press on, and what does the FOM require?
a: No. In the event of required RVSM equipment failure prior to or within RVSM airspace, notify ATC and Dispatch to coordinate a prudent course of action. ATC may not require any action, but a reroute or diversion may be required. Both primary altimeters and one autopilot altitude-control system must be operating normally for RVSM; the standby altimeter may not be used as a primary.

src.quote: In the event of required RVSM equipment failure prior to or within RVSM airspace, notify ATC and Dispatch to coordinate a prudent course of action. ATC may not require any action; however, a reroute or diversion may be required.
src.note: Required RVSM equipment includes both primary altimeters, one autopilot altitude-control system, and the altitude alerting system; loss of any of these drives the ATC/Dispatch coordination, and the standby altimeter is prohibited as a primary.

q: SCENARIO (check airman): Landing rollout complete, the RVR is 900 and dropping in dense fog. The First Officer offers to taxi to the gate while the Captain runs the after-landing flow. Is that acceptable, and how are checklists handled?
a: No. RVR 900 is below 1200, so this is restricted/low visibility. During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft, not the First Officer. Checklists are performed with the aircraft stopped and the parking brake set, all exterior lights except landing lights are on, and maximum attention is devoted to scanning outside while taxiing.

src.quote: During low visibility operations, the Captain must taxi the aircraft.
src.note: Restricted visibility includes any time RVR is less than 1200; the Captain taxis, checklists are done stopped with the parking brake set, and no taxiing-unrelated duties are performed until stopped.

q: Rev 125: how is A330 operational/in-flight landing distance now calculated, and what safety margin applies?
a: On TALPA guidance, using a 7-second air/flare distance from 50 ft above the runway threshold to touchdown. A 15% safety margin is applied to total landing distance, including the air distance, for both maximum manual braking and autobrake. The touchdown point is not a fixed distance; it is calculated and varies with weight, pressure altitude, temperature, approach speed, and wind.

src.quote: (717/787/A321/A330) Operational/In-flight landing distance calculations are based on TALPA guidance, using a 7-second air/flare distance (from 50 ft above runway threshold to touchdown). A 15% safety margin is applied to total landing distance, including the air distance, for both maximum manual braking and autobrake configurations. The touchdown point is not a fixed distance but rather a calculated value that varies with landing conditions such as aircraft weight, pressure altitude, temperature, approach speed, and wind.
src.note: New in Rev 125 and bannered (717/787/A321/A330). The old fixed touchdown-point model is now banner-tagged (737) and no longer describes the A330.

q: Rev 125: after 'Cabin Secure' and Flight Deck Door closure, what must the Flight Crew confirm before the aircraft moves?
a: All door indications closed, verbal confirmation from the Ground Crew that the Walkaround Check is complete, and, if installed, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) verified stowed and latched.

src.ref: FOM 5.2.20 - Cabin Safety Check Prior to Taxi or Pushback
src.quote: The Flight Crew must check all door indications to confirm they are closed and receive a verbal confirmation from the Ground Crew that the Walkaround Check is complete. If installed, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) must be verified stowed and latched.
src.note: The IPSB sentence is NEW in Rev 125.

q: When should the APU be started before pushback?
a: 10 minutes prior to the anticipated pushback, unless it is required earlier for passenger comfort or equipment (PCA or external power) issues.

src.quote: The APU should be started 10 minutes prior to the anticipated pushback, unless it is required for passenger comfort or equipment (PCA or external power) issues.
src.note: Rev 125 made this all-fleet. Prioritize ground-supplied preconditioned air; if external power or PCA is not connected on arrival at the aircraft, call Ops before starting the APU.

q: On the A330, how far may a cabin door be opened without fall protection in place?
a: Not any distance. On the 717/787/A321/A330, cabin doors must not be opened any distance without proper fall protection in place prior to door opening (the 737 allowance is 12 inches).

src.quote: (717/787/A321/A330) Cabin doors must not be opened any distance without proper fall protection in place prior to door opening.
src.note: Relevant when no Cabin Crew is on board, such as ferry or check flights.

q: If potable water had to be drained and cannot be refilled (for example in extreme cold), is an MEL required to operate without it?
a: No. In these instances an MEL does not need to be applied to operate without potable water.

src.quote: In rare conditions, the water may need to be drained and cannot be refilled (e.g., extreme cold temperatures). In these instances, an MEL does not need to be applied to operate without potable water.
src.note: Rev 125. Whether to operate without potable water is otherwise at the Captain's discretion considering flight time, passenger load, and availability of bottled water, wipes and hand sanitizer.

q: When must a broadband (entertainment system) outage be written up in the Maintenance Logbook?
a: If the broadband system drops offline and does not automatically reestablish internet connectivity before the end of the flight, write it up at the completion of the flight.

src.quote: If the broadband system drops offline and does not automatically reestablish internet connectivity before the end of the flight, it should be written up in the Maintenance Logbook at the completion of the flight.
src.note: New section in Rev 125. Short intermittent dropouts due to reception are expected and need no write-up.

q: On the A330, how many Flight Crew and how many Cabin Crew may use the Lower Deck Module Crew Rest (LDMCR) at any time, and which bunks are the Flight Crew bunks?
a: No more than 2 Flight Crew and 4 Cabin Crew at any time. Bunks 1 and 4 are reserved for Flight Crew and non-revenue HA pilots; bunks 2, 3, 5, and 6 are for Cabin Crew.

src.quote: There are 2 bunks (1 and 4) reserved for Flight Crew and non-revenue HA pilots, and 4 bunks (2, 3, 5, and 6) reserved for Cabin Crew. Flight Crew and non-revenue HA pilots must not use bunks 2, 3, 5, or 6, and Cabin Crew must not use bunks 1 or 4. The FAA requires Flight Crew sleeping quarters to meet certain minimum standards, and only bunks 1 and 4 meet these standards. No more than 2 Flight Crew and 4 Cabin Crew are authorized to use the LDMCR at any time.
src.note: Only bunks 1 and 4 meet the FAA Flight Crew sleeping-quarter standard. Use PA+ALL and the handset push-to-talk to make a cabin PA without disturbing the LDMCR.

q: On an A330 with all LDMCR available, which pilot crew rest seats must be blocked for an Augmented Crew?
a: Hard block 3C or 3G, with the other of 3C or 3G as last sold/last assigned. For a Double Augmented or Double Crew, hard block both 3C and 3G.

src.quote: A330 – All LDMCR Available Hard Blocked: 3C or 3G Last Sold/Last Assigned: 3C or 3G, whichever is not hard Hard Blocked: 3C and 3G blocked
src.note: Table 5.1.23.8.1(1) cells run together in the text extract; the Augmented column is 3C or 3G hard blocked plus the other last sold, the Double column is 3C and 3G hard blocked. Pilot crew rest seats are required on all Augmented, Double Augmented, or Double Crew flights.

q: If the decision is made to deplane during boarding or before departure, who should be notified first and why?
a: The CSA, before deplaning begins, to give the station time to prepare (open the flight, coordinate installation of a tail stand).

src.quote: If during the boarding process or prior to departure the decision to deplane is made, the CSA should be notified before deplaning begins to give station time to prepare (e.g., open the flight, coordinate installation of tail stand).
src.note: Rev 125 addition.

q: When and to what address do you log on CPDLC for Iceland?
a: Climbing through FL100, logon address BIRD.

src.quote: Iceland Climbing through FL100 BIRD
src.note: Iceland was added to the logon table in Rev 125. Japan and New Zealand are climbing through 10k (RJJJ, NZZO); Mexico is during preflight (KUSA); South Korea is east of Japan (RJJJ); Tahiti climbing through 10k (NTTT).

q: On the A330, is a forward tow permitted with both engines running?
a: No. For the 787 and A330 the Ground Crew policy currently prohibits forward tow operations with both engines running.

src.quote: (787/A330) The Ground Crew policy currently prohibits forward tow operations with both engines running.
src.note: The Marshaller may also delay engine start until pushback is complete if ramp conditions do not permit.

q: On a visual approach with an instrument approach available to the landing runway, what must the pilots do with the navaid and FMS?
a: Tune, identify, and monitor the appropriate navigational aid and/or program the FMS as a backup for guidance. This is mandatory; the time-permitting qualifier was removed in Rev 125.

src.quote: When an instrument approach is available to the runway of intended landing, pilots shall tune, identify, and monitor the appropriate navigational aid and/or program the FMC/FMS as a backup for guidance.
src.note: Rev 125 changed this from a time-permitting recommendation to a shall.

q: On the A330, when may a VNAV approach be flown to a DA(H) in lieu of the published MDA(H)?
a: When the chart contains a note stating "Only authorized operators may use VNAV DA(H) in lieu of MDA(H)" or "VNAV DA(H) in lieu of MDA(H) depends on operator policy." Refer to the fleet-specific manuals for procedures.

src.ref: FOM 5.6.14.1, VNAV Approaches Using DA in lieu of MDA (787/A321/A330)
src.quote: VNAV approaches may be flown to the published MDA(H) if the chart contains a note stating: • “Only authorized operators may use VNAV DA(H) in lieu of MDA(H),” or • “VNAV DA(H) in lieu of MDA(H) depends on operator policy.” Refer to the fleet-specific manuals for procedures.
src.note: Ops Spec C073. Bannered (787/A321/A330).

q: On the A330, is a one-engine-inoperative CAT II Autoland authorized? A CAT III?
a: CAT II yes: Ops Spec authorization allows one-engine inoperative CAT II Autoland on the A321/A330. CAT III no: one-engine CAT III Autoland is not authorized.

src.ref: FOM 5.6.17.2 and 5.6.17.3, CAT II and CAT III Operating Limitations
src.quote: (A321/A330) Ops Spec authorization allows for one-engine inoperative CAT II Autoland.
src.note: The CAT III bullet reads: (A321/A330) One-engine CAT III Autoland is not authorized.

q: For Autoland operations on the A330, what qualification must the PIC hold, and on which runways are Autolands permitted?
a: The PIC must be Autoland qualified (787/A321/A330). Autoland approaches and landings are permitted on CAT II/III runways only, and pilots should advise the tower so the ILS critical zone is protected.

src.quote: (787/A321/A330) The PIC must be Autoland qualified.
src.note: Ops Spec C061. The ILS critical area is normally protected when the weather is below 800 ft or 2 miles.

q: How must non-normal (abnormal) landing data be treated when determining runway suitability?
a: Unfactored data (no safety buffer) represents actual aircraft performance and must be considered the minimum acceptable limit.

src.quote: Unfactored data (with no safety buffer) represents actual aircraft performance and must be considered the minimum acceptable limit.
src.note: Rev 125 made this all-fleet. Non-normal data may still be used for abnormals to determine runway suitability.

q: On the A330, below what height AGL must fuel jettison be avoided, and what ATC notifications are required?
a: Avoid jettisoning below 6000 ft AGL (also near cities and towns, into the jettisoned flow, and near thunderstorms). Notify ATC before starting jettison and when complete, and coordinate route, altitude, and duration.

src.quote: In the event the Captain elects to jettison fuel, the Flight Crew should minimize potentially adverse effects to humans, animals, or vegetation and avoid jettisoning: • Below 6000 ft AGL • Near cities and towns, and preferably remain over water • Into the jettisoned flow (which descends at about 500 ft/min) • Near areas where thunderstorms have been reported or are expected The Flight Crew must notify ATC prior to starting fuel jettison and when jettison is complete.
src.note: After jettisoning, complete a Pilot Report of Incident with date, time, and approximate amount jettisoned.

q: If a hard landing is suspected, what two actions does the FOM require?
a: Make a Maintenance Logbook entry, ensuring the defect description notes that it was a hard landing, and submit a safety report.

src.quote: Make a Maintenance Logbook entry, ensuring that in the defect description it is notated that it was a hard landing. • Submit a safety report.
src.note: A landing does not need to be overweight to be considered hard.

q: What ground personnel are required to park an A330 (manual or VDGS), and where are station exceptions published?
a: Two Wing Walkers and one Marshaller/VDGS Operator for the 787/A330. Station-specific exceptions to the two Wing Walker requirement are denoted in the airport 10-7.

src.quote: (787/A330) Two Wing Walkers and One Marshaller/VDGS Operator Station-specific exceptions to the requirement to have two Wing Walkers will be denoted in the airport 10-7.
src.note: Rev 125 added the 10-7 exception wording. Local policies may require more personnel than the minimum.

q: Approximately 2 minutes before an oceanic waypoint, what must the crew confirm?
a: That the upcoming waypoint and the subsequent waypoint (next + 1) agree with the Flight Plan/ATC clearance.

src.quote: Approximately 2 minutes prior to reaching a waypoint, confirm that the upcoming waypoint and the subsequent waypoint (next + 1) agrees with the Flight Plan/ATC clearance.
src.note: Rev 125 added the next + 1 requirement. After transition, record time and fuel from the FMS and compare with the estimates.

q: On CPDLC in oceanic airspace, what is required if SELCAL is not functioning?
a: One member of the crew must listen to HF continuously.

src.quote: If SELCAL is not functioning, one member of the crew must listen to HF continuously.
src.note: Rev 125. SELCAL codes are also not unique (20.4.3.1): verify the callsign before responding.

q: How does the FOM define an ETOPS operation in terms of distance from an adequate airport?
a: A flight that operates over a route containing a point farther than 60 minutes of flying time from an adequate airport, at an approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air.

src.quote: flights that operate over a route that contains a point farther than 60 minutes of flying time from an adequate airport, at an approved one-engine inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air
src.note: This 60-minute threshold is the trigger for ETOPS. The one-engine-inoperative cruise speed used to measure it is the A330 fleet value of .82M/290 KIAS (6.2.3).

q: What distance defines an Extended Over-Water Operation?
a: An operation over water at a horizontal distance of more than 50 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline.
