src.quote: An operation over water at a horizontal distance of more than 50 nautical miles from the nearest shoreline.
src.note: Do not confuse the 50 NM over-water trigger with the 60-minute ETOPS trigger; they are separate concepts.

q: What is the two-part premise of ETOPS philosophy?
a: To preclude a diversion and, if one were to occur, to have programs in place to protect the diversion.

src.ref: FOM 6.1.3, ETOPS Philosophy: Preclude and Protect
src.quote: The premise of ETOPS is to preclude a diversion and, if it were to occur, to have programs in place to protect the diversion.
src.note: Preclude layers include design, testing, maintenance, and flight ops procedures; protect layers include monitored alternates, enhanced comms, and enhanced dispatch fuel.

q: For an adequate airport, within what portion of runway length must a turbojet be able to stop, and from what height?
a: Within 60 percent of the effective length of a runway, measured from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway.

src.quote: Turbojet aircraft must be able to be stopped within 60 percent of the effective length of a runway from a point 50 ft above the intersection of the obstruction clearance plane and the runway.
src.note: An adequate airport must also meet 14 CFR 121.197 landing limitations and Part 139 Subpart D (excluding ARFF), or be an active military airport.

q: What minimum rescue and firefighting (RFFS) category must each designated ETOPS alternate airport have?
a: RFFS equivalent to that specified by ICAO as Category 4, or higher.

src.quote: rescue and firefighting service (RFFS) equivalent to that specified by ICAO as Category 4, or higher
src.note: Note the distinction: an adequate airport does not require ARFF, but a designated ETOPS alternate must have at least ICAO Category 4 RFFS.

q: What firefighting response time must an FAA-approved ETOPS alternate meet, and what does it actually require?
a: A 30-minute response time. It does not require equipment to be pre-positioned; it means firefighting equipment must be available on arrival of the diverting airplane and remain on station as long as needed.

src.quote: firefighting assistance within a 30-minute response time
src.note: The FOM clarifies the 30-minute response time means equipment available on arrival of the diverting airplane, not standing by for 30 minutes beforehand.

q: What is Alaska Airlines' authorized Maximum Diversion Time (MDT), and where does the ETOPS area of operation begin?
a: The authorized MDT is 180 minutes. The ETOPS area of operation begins beyond 60 minutes from the adequate airport and extends to the planned MDT from the planned ETOPS alternates.

src.quote: The Alaska Airlines’ authorized MDT is 180 minutes.
src.note: MDT is computed at one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air, and the MDT the flight was planned on must be listed in the Dispatch Release.

q: For ETOPS up to and including 180 minutes, the time to an ETOPS alternate may not exceed what limit?
a: It may not exceed the approved time for the aircraft's most limiting ETOPS-significant system (including the most limiting fire-suppression system time for compartments required to have fire suppression) minus 15 minutes.

src.quote: would exceed the approved time for the aircraft’s most limiting ETOPS-significant system (including the aircraft’s most limiting fire-suppression system time for those cargo and baggage compartments required by regulation to have fire-suppression systems) minus 15 minutes.
src.note: This 'minus 15 minutes' buffer also appears in 6.2.5 as the ceiling on actual diversion time per 14 CFR 121.633.

q: What can occasionally reduce the MDT to 120 minutes, and what is the maximum diversion time to an ETOPS alternate from any point along the route?
a: MEL-deferred items may occasionally limit the MDT to 120 minutes. The diversion time from any point along the route must be no more than 120 or 180 minutes (as dispatched) to the ETOPS alternate.

src.quote: Occasionally, MEL-deferred items may limit the MDT to 120 minutes.
src.note: This diversion time is measured at one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air and yields a fixed Maximum Diversion Distance (MDD) per aircraft.

q: For the A330-200, what single-engine speed and what flying distances correspond to the 60-, 120-, and 180-minute rings?
a: A330-200: .82M/290 KIAS, giving 408 nm at 60 minutes, 803 nm at 120 minutes, and 1200 nm at 180 minutes.

src.ref: FOM 6.2.3, Table 6.2.3(1): ETOPS Area of Operations
src.note: These are the fixed A330-200 distances that define the range rings; the 60-minute ring (408 nm) marks the EEP/EXP distance. Table 6.2.3 also lists the A330-300F at 405/792/1183 nm.

q: What are the three critical fuel scenarios used to compute fuel to fly to an ETOPS alternate?
a: (1) Immediate descent from cruise to 10,000 ft with both engines operating (pressurization loss); (2) descent to best single-engine altitude with one engine operating (engine failure); (3) immediate descent to 10,000 ft with one engine operating (simultaneous pressurization loss and engine failure).

src.quote: An immediate descent to 10,000 ft with one engine operating (pressurization loss and simultaneous engine-failure scenario)
src.note: The fuel calculation uses the most critical of these scenarios from the critical point (CP/ETP) to the diversion airport.

q: Upon reaching the ETOPS alternate, what fuel allowance does the critical fuel calculation include?
a: Fuel to descend to 1500 ft above the airport, hold for 15 minutes, and then conduct an instrument approach and landing.

src.quote: Fuel to descend to 1500 ft above the airport, hold for 15 minutes, and then conduct an instrument approach and landing.
src.note: This arrival allowance is one element added on top of the fuel to fly to the alternate under the critical scenario.

q: How is forecast wind adjusted in the ETOPS critical fuel calculation?
a: Forecast wind speeds are increased by 5%, resulting in an increase in headwind or a decrease in tailwind.

src.quote: forecast wind speeds which have been increased by 5% (resulting in an increase in headwind or a decrease in tailwind)
src.note: This is one of several conservative adjustments, alongside icing, engine deterioration, APU use, and MEL/CDL penalties.

q: What does the '(AS) ER or ETOPS' designation mean in the MEL, and how is it typically used?
a: It refers to Extended Operations of a two-engine aircraft with a type design approval for ETOPS. The designation is used primarily as an exception to a normally allowed MEL deferred item.

src.quote: The ER or ETOPS designation is used primarily as an exception to a normally allowed MEL deferred item.
src.note: MEL ETOPS-critical items may limit the ETOPS area of operations or preclude ETOPS entirely; compliance with the MEL is a critical factor in ETOPS.

q: For the A330, what one-engine-inoperative reference speed, reference weight, and reference flight level are used to derive ETOPS speeds?
a: A330: .82M/290 KIAS, a reference weight of 470,000 lb, and reference FL350.

src.note: Reference weights and OEI flight levels derive the EEP/EXP distance and ETOPS area of operation for each fleet. For dispatch planning, actual planned weights are used.

q: How long does the ETOPS Dispatch Release / Pre-Departure Check remain valid, and what is required after that?
a: It remains valid for four hours after the scheduled departure time. After the release expiration, a new Pre-Departure Check and an amended Dispatch Release are required.

src.ref: FOM 6.3.2, Flight Crew Duties / ETOPS Dispatch Release
src.quote: A new Pre-Departure Check and amended Dispatch Release are required after the valid time (release expiration), which is four hours after the scheduled departure time.
src.note: 'ETOPS NA' on the release indicates the aircraft is not ETOPS capable; the 'EQUIP ETOPS' line is not an indication of ETOPS status.

q: When does the aircraft reach the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP), and how is the EXP distance related?
a: The EEP is reached when the aircraft is 60 minutes from the adequate airport (at OEI cruise speed, standard conditions, still air). The EXP represents the same 60-minute distance and results in the same fixed distance as the EEP.

src.ref: FOM 6.3.3, ETOPS Entry/Exit Point/Equal Time Point
src.quote: reaches the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP) when it is 60 minutes from the adequate airport
src.note: Flight Crew and Dispatch must use the same adequate airports to define EEP and EXP, and those airports must be listed on the Dispatch Release.

q: Do ETOPS regulations add fuel requirements once in flight, and what does arriving at the CP/ETP below critical fuel actually require?
a: No; ETOPS regulations do not add any additional fuel requirements once in flight. Arriving at the CP/ETP at or above critical fuel is only a dispatch requirement, so there is no requirement to divert prior to the CP for that reason alone, provided estimated fuel at destination is above arrival requirements.

src.quote: ETOPS regulations do not add any additional fuel requirements once in flight.
src.note: Fuel monitoring remains critical given the potential for a long diversion; the Dispatcher may adjust altitude, speed, enroute alternate, and routing to meet the critical fuel requirement.

q: At what altitude and winds does Alaska calculate Equal-Time Points (ETPs), and what is an ETP?
a: ETPs are calculated using flight performance and winds at 10,000 ft. An ETP is a point where the flight time, considering wind, to each of two selected diversion destinations is equal.

src.quote: ETPs are calculated using flight performance and winds at 10,000 ft.
src.note: Because ETPs are wind-affected, a different ETP exists for each altitude; crews should also stay aware of the airport that takes the least time to reach near cruise altitude.

q: Within what timeframe must ETOPS discrepancies such as IFSDs and diversions be reported?
a: Within 96 hours.

src.quote: Within 96 hours, the certificate holder must report IFSDs, diversions/turnbacks for failures/malfunctions/defects
src.note: Reportable events include uncommanded thrust changes, inability to control thrust, fuel loss/imbalance, and any event jeopardizing safe flight and landing; prompt crew reporting helps meet this requirement.

q: Before the EEP, what ETOPS-specific duty does the Dispatcher perform for the ETOPS alternates?
a: Provide via ACARS, SATCOM, or HF any relevant updates to weather and/or safety of flight NOTAMs for the ETOPS alternate airports.

src.quote: Before EEP Provide via ACARS, SATCOM, or HF any relevant updates to weather and/or safety of flight NOTAMs for ETOPS alternate airports.
src.note: Enroute the Dispatcher evaluates weather, NOTAMs and field conditions at each designated ETOPS alternate from earliest to latest arrival time, watches for fuel-consumption variance, and relays significant changes. The FOM does not state a crew-acknowledgement requirement.

q: What is the ETOPS Dual Maintenance Limitation?
a: Restrictions are placed on performing dual maintenance on ETOPS Significant Systems to prevent failures.

src.quote: Dual Maintenance Limitations: Restrictions are placed on performing dual maintenance on ETOPS Significant Systems to prevent failures.
src.note: Part of the ETOPS maintenance program (6.5.1) alongside the Verification Program and Monitoring Programs.

q: What three checks does the ETOPS Pre-Departure Service Check (PDSC) include at minimum?
a: Verification of the condition of all ETOPS Significant Systems; verification of the overall status of the aircraft by reviewing applicable maintenance records; and an interior and exterior inspection including engine and APU oil levels and consumption rates.

src.quote: • Verification of the condition of all ETOPS Significant Systems (see 6.5.3 – ETOPS Significant Systems) • Verification of the overall status of the aircraft by reviewing applicable maintenance records • An interior and exterior inspection to include a determination of engine and APU oil levels and consumption rates
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.4, these are exactly the three minimum PDC/PDSC elements. Primary responsibility lies with Maintenance; an ETOPS-qualified mechanic must sign the logbook prior to ETOPS operation.

q: What weather condition must be met before the Dispatcher lists an airport as an ETOPS alternate on the Dispatch Release?
a: The appropriate weather reports or forecasts, or any combination, must indicate the weather will be at or above the ETOPS alternate airport minima specified in Ops Spec C055 from the earliest to the latest time of arrival.

src.quote: The Dispatcher will not list an airport as an ETOPS alternate airport on the Dispatch Release unless: • The appropriate weather reports or forecasts, or any combination thereof, indicate that the weather conditions will be at or above the ETOPS alternate airport minima specified in Ops Spec
src.note: The airport must also be an adequate airport listed in 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports, and field condition reports must indicate a safe landing can be made.

q: Check-airman scenario: You are 8 minutes from the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP) on the A330 to Honolulu when Dispatch relays that your designated ETOPS alternate's weather has just dropped below the crew's operating minima and no METAR is coming. What is required, and how would it differ if this happened AFTER the EEP?
a: Before the EEP: you must have a suitable ETOPS alternate to enter the ETOPS area. Coordinate with Dispatch to establish a new ETOPS alternate; if none can be designated (and the existing one is no longer available), a turnback is required before crossing the EEP. After the EEP: a turnback is NOT required just because the alternate is below the crew's operating minima or the runway is unusable, you attempt to establish a new ETOPS alternate with Dispatch, which may lead to a turnback, reroute, or continuation, and the PIC and Dispatcher exercise judgment on the safest course.

src.ref: FOM 6.3.5, In-Flight ETOPS Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
src.quote: • A turnback is required if an ETOPS alternate is no longer available. After the EEP: • A turnback is not required if weather at the ETOPS alternate is below the crew’s operating minima or the runway is unusable. • If required, attempt to establish a new ETOPS alternate with Dispatch which may lead to a turnback, reroute, or continuation on planned route.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.3.5. The EEP is the hinge: pre-EEP the alternate must be suitable to enter; post-EEP the crew and Dispatch work the problem in flight rather than automatically turning back.

q: Check-airman scenario: Cruising the CEP between two ETOPS alternates, you pass the fuel-critical Equal-Time Point (ETP) and a few minutes later get a single-engine event. Which airport, what speed, and what's the governing rule?
a: Divert to the nearest SUITABLE airport in the Captain's judgment (14 CFR 121.565). By definition of the ETP, once you are past it the airport ahead now takes the least time, so it is generally the diversion field. Fly the approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed, .82M/290 KIAS for the A330, which is the planned diversion speed; the Captain may deviate only after assessing the emergency and considering fuel remaining. The ETP is a wind-based planning point (Alaska computes ETPs at 10,000 ft) and the flight-planning system does not account for the time and fuel to make the 180 degree turn near the ETP.

src.quote: 14 CFR 121.565 requires the Captain of a two-engine aircraft with one engine inoperative to land at the nearest suitable airport where, in the Captain’s judgment after considering all relevant factors, a safe landing can be made.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.4.2 (nearest suitable), 6.4.5 (OEI cruise speed = the planned diversion speed; Captain may deviate after assessing emergency and fuel), 6.3.7 (ETP is per-altitude, wind-affected, computed at 10,000 ft), and 6.4.1 (turn time/fuel near a fuel-critical ETP is not modeled by the flight-planning system).

q: Check-airman scenario: Maintenance signs the ETOPS PDSC at 0400Z. A gate hold pushes departure late. Walk through what happens if boarding began at 0730Z versus if, at 0800Z, boarding still hasn't started.
a: The PDSC Airworthiness Release is valid four hours from the sign-off time (0400Z to 0800Z). If boarding began before the four hours lapsed (0730Z is inside the window), the flight may continue on the existing PDSC, but the flight must notify MOC. If, at the end of the four hours (0800Z), the aircraft isn't ready and boarding has NOT started, the PDSC is invalidated and a new PDSC is required. MOC monitors the four-hour clock and notifies Maintenance and SOCC/Dispatch if a new PDSC is needed. Separately, if the crew suspects a maintenance action invalidated the PDSC, they contact MOC via Dispatch.

src.quote: An ETOPS PDSC Airworthiness Release will be valid for four (4) hours from the time the Airworthiness Release block was signed in the M258 Aircraft Maintenance Logbook. If, at the end of four (4) hours, the flight or aircraft is not ready for departure and boarding has not started, the PDSC is invalidated.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.5.4. Do not confuse this maintenance PDSC 4-hour clock (from logbook sign-off) with the Dispatch Release/PDC validity, which runs four hours from the scheduled departure time (6.3.2 / 6.5.4).

q: Check-airman scenario: Still short of the EEP, your fuel readout suggests estimated fuel on board at the CP/ETP will come in below the critical-fuel-scenario figure on the release. Are you required to divert before the critical point?
a: No. Arriving at the CP/ETP with fuel on board at or above the critical fuel scenario is only a DISPATCH requirement, ETOPS regulations add no additional fuel requirement once in flight. If it appears estimated FOB at the CP/ETP will be low, there is no requirement to divert prior to the CP for that reason alone, provided estimated fuel at destination is above the arrival requirements. The Dispatcher should evaluate changes to altitude, speed, enroute alternate, and routing to try to meet the flight plan's critical fuel requirement, though it may not always be possible. Keep monitoring fuel closely given the potential for a long diversion.

src.quote: ETOPS regulations do not add any additional fuel requirements once in flight.
src.note: VERIFIED in ch6.txt 6.3.6. The critical fuel is planned from the CP/ETP to the diversion airport using the worst of three scenarios (both engines to 10,000 ft; one engine to best single-engine altitude; one engine to 10,000 ft) plus a 1,500 ft / 15-minute hold / approach-and-land allowance, winds increased 5% (6.2.5).

q: Under FOM 125.1, which airports may be used as an adequate airport for ETOPS planning?
a: Any regular, provisional, refueling, or alternate airport listed in 8.1.3 Authorized Airports, provided the 6.2.1 criteria are met.

src.quote: Any regular, provisional, refueling, or alternate airport may be used as an adequate airport provided it is listed in 8.1.3 – Authorized Airports.
src.note: Rev 125 re-pointed the definition from OpSpec B342/C070 to the single 8.1.3 table. An adequate airport may still be inappropriate for an actual diversion (RFFS, weather).

q: Before the EEP on an HA A330 ETOPS flight, what must be complete regarding ETOPS verification?
a: Complete any ETOPS verification flight checks (787/A321/A330).

src.ref: FOM 6.3.5, Prior to Crossing ETOPS Entry Point (EEP)
src.quote: (787/A321/A330) Complete any ETOPS verification flight checks.
src.note: The 737 line instead requires ETOPS system verification, Maintenance Control notification and an amended release. After the EEP (HA), monitor distance from an ETOPS alternate to stay within the ETOPS area of operation.

q: Once airborne (in-flight operations), who is the flight crew's primary contact for requests and notifications?
a: The Dispatcher, who both manages information flow and shares operational control with the Captain.

src.quote: The Dispatcher is the primary contact for requests and notifications, both managing information flow and sharing operational control with the Captain.
src.note: On the ground the primary contact is Station ground personnel (7.1.1.1); once in flight it shifts to the Dispatcher. Maintenance will not normally communicate directly with an airborne aircraft.

q: When operating with CPDLC, in what airspace is free text supported?
a: Free text is only supported in oceanic airspace; free text in domestic airspace is not supported.

src.ref: FOM 7.1.2.1, Common Language and Standard Phraseology
src.quote: text is only supported in oceanic airspace. Only use standard aviation terminology. Free text in domestic airspace is not supported.
src.note: Domestic CPDLC requires standard aviation terminology only. Free text is an oceanic-only capability.

q: For operations outside the US, to which aircraft does the word "Heavy" apply and when must it be used?
a: Aircraft capable of takeoff with weights of 300,000 lbs or more; required only upon initial contact with the tower and approach/departure control (and on each new frequency initial contact over Canadian airspace).

src.quote: For operations outside of the US, the word “Heavy” applies to aircraft capable of takeoff with weights of 300,000 lbs or more and is only required upon initial contact with the tower and approach/departure control.
src.note: In the US terminal area the 787 and A330 must add "Heavy" to the call sign in all air/ground communications; it is not required during enroute communications.

q: Below what altitude are flight crewmembers required to use a boom microphone?
a: Below 18,000 ft. Above FL180, use of loudspeakers or headsets is at the PIC's discretion.

src.quote: Flight Crewmembers are required to use a boom microphone below 18,000 ft.
src.note: Reference is 14 CFR 121.359. The loudspeaker is not used when the PA is used from the Flight Deck or when headsets are worn.

q: How are the three VHF comm radios normally prioritized, and what does #2/R monitor?
a: #1/L is primary communications, #2/R is departure/enroute/arrival and monitors 121.5 (Company on the ground), and #3/C is ACARS.

src.quote: #2/R VHF – Departure/Enroute/Arrival: Monitor 121.5
src.note: In flight within the state of Alaska, the Company frequency should normally be monitored on the #2 VHF. #3/C is dedicated to ACARS.

q: What is the restriction on operating HF radios during fueling?
a: Do not operate HF radios during fueling operations.

src.quote: Do not operate HF radios during fueling operations.
src.note: FCC regulations prohibit regular HF use within the continental US, though HF radio checks are permitted. This warning is a fueling-safety item.

q: Is routine satellite (SATCOM) voice communication with ATC authorized?
a: No. Routine satellite voice communication with ATC is not authorized; however, it may be used when HF or CPDLC are not available.

src.quote: Routine satellite voice communication with ATC is not authorized; however, it may be used when HF or CPDLC are not available.
src.note: Satellite voice with Dispatch or MedLink is at the pilot's discretion. SATCOM is generally less reliable than HF in polar regions.

q: For NAT HLA oceanic airspace, what flight levels does the Data Link Mandate (DLM) cover and what capabilities are required for dispatch?
a: Flight Levels 290-410 inclusive; the aircraft must be dispatched with ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link capabilities.

src.ref: FOM 7.1.8.1, NAT HLA Data Link Mandate (DLM)
src.quote: a Data Link Mandate (DLM) is in effect for Flight Levels 290-410, inclusive. The DLM requires that aircraft must be dispatched with ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link capabilities.
src.note: The DLM applies to operations in NAT HLA Oceanic airspace.

q: How many crewmembers should be present to accept an ATC clearance, and what abbreviated-clearance restriction applies to the Captain?
a: At least two crewmembers should be present to monitor and confirm an ATC clearance; the Captain must not accept an abbreviated clearance if the filed Flight Plan was changed prior to departure.

src.quote: At least two crewmembers should be present to monitor and confirm an ATC clearance.
src.note: When two-crew confirmation is not feasible, crewmembers must ensure a mutual understanding of the latest clearance.

q: Under Radio Reports to ATC, at what minimum climb/descent performance must you notify ATC?
a: Report to ATC if unable to climb or descend at least 500 ft per minute.

src.quote: If unable to climb or descend at least 500 ft per minute
src.note: One of the reports that should be made to ATC at all times, alongside vacating an altitude, missed approach, and reaching/leaving a holding fix.

q: At cruise, what change in true airspeed requires a report to ATC?
a: A change in TAS at cruise of more than 5%, 10 kts, or 0.02 Mach from Flight Plan speed.

src.quote: Change in TAS at cruise of more than 5%, 10 kts, or 0.02 Mach from Flight Plan speed
src.note: A required ATC report at all times. Any of the three thresholds triggers the report.

q: When not in radar contact, when must a corrected time estimate be reported to ATC?
a: When a previous estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes (3 minutes or more in NAT HLA).

src.quote: A corrected estimate when a previous estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes (3 minutes or more in NAT HLA)
src.note: This is one of the additional reports required specifically when not in radar contact.

q: By how much must actual fuel remaining differ from planned before contacting Dispatch on the A330?
a: By plus or minus 3000 lbs on the A330 (and 787). The 717, 737 and A321 threshold is plus or minus 2000 lbs.

src.note: Contact Dispatch as safety-of-flight considerations permit; notification is mandatory but timing is workload-dependent.

q: What thresholds define a "significant" deviation from the Flight Plan that requires contacting Dispatch?
a: Lateral deviation of 100 nm or more from the planned route, altitude deviation of 4000 ft or more from planned cruise altitude, or any action likely to delay arrival by more than 15 minutes.

src.quote: Lateral deviation: 100 nm or more from the planned route.
src.note: The same section requires contacting Dispatch for moderate or greater turbulence and for mechanical irregularities that could interrupt the schedule.

q: By approximately what altitudes must the sterile flight deck chimes (two distinct chimes) be given on departure and arrival?
a: By approximately 10,000 ft MSL during departure and 10,000 ft AFE during arrival.

src.ref: FOM 7.1.20.3, Sterile Flight Deck Operations Advisory
src.quote: shall always be cycled to produce two distinct chimes by approximately 10,000 ft MSL during departure and 10,000 ft AFE during arrival.
src.note: On the A330 (and 717/A321) this is the No Smoking Switch; on the 737 the Fasten Seat Belts Switch. The chime is mandatory even if the cabin was already prepared for arrival due to turbulence.

q: How long before takeoff should the verbatim Impending Takeoff Advisory ("Flight Attendants should now be seated for takeoff") be made?
a: At least 2 minutes prior to takeoff, prior to taking position on an active runway.

src.quote: This announcement should be made at least 2 minutes prior to takeoff.
src.note: It is a verbatim announcement and must not be combined with any other announcement.

q: By when must a safety report for an NTSB reportable item be filed?
a: No later than the end of the next 24-hour rest period.

src.quote: A safety report for an NTSB reportable item must be filed no later than the end of the next 24-hour rest period.
src.note: NTSB-reportable events include in-flight fire/smoke, flight control malfunction, near midair collision, and a TCAS RA where compliance was necessary to avert substantial collision risk.

q: Under ASAP, what is the phone number and the deadline for the follow-up written report and for submitting the report?
a: Call 877-897-ASAP (2727); the phone call must be followed by a written report within 24 hours of the call, and ASAP reports should be submitted within 24 hours from the end of that day's flight sequence.

src.quote: The phone call must be followed by a written report within 24 hours of the call.
src.note: ASAP uses an FAA non-punitive incentive to encourage reporting and does not replace the safety report or the NASA ASRS form.

q: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are dispatched for a North Atlantic crossing planning FL350 through NAT HLA Oceanic airspace, but the release shows the aircraft's SATCOM data link is inoperative. May you accept an oceanic clearance into the organized track system at FL350?
a: No. In NAT HLA Oceanic airspace a Data Link Mandate is in effect for FL290-410 inclusive, and it requires the aircraft be dispatched with ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link. Without working SATCOM data link you cannot operate in that DLM band.

src.ref: FOM 7.1.8.1, NAT HLA Data Link Mandate (DLM)
src.quote: For operations in NAT HLA Oceanic airspace, a Data Link Mandate (DLM) is in effect for Flight Levels 290-410, inclusive. The DLM requires that aircraft must be dispatched with ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link capabilities.
src.note: All three capabilities, ADS-C, CPDLC, and SATCOM data link, are required together for the FL290-410 mandate.

q: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: Oceanic and not in radar contact in NAT HLA, your previous estimate for the next waypoint is now going to be off by about 2.5 minutes. Do you owe ATC a corrected estimate?
a: No, not on that basis. When not in radar contact a corrected estimate is required when the previous estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes, but in NAT HLA the threshold is 3 minutes or more; a 2.5-minute error does not trigger the corrected estimate in NAT HLA.

src.quote: A corrected estimate when a previous estimate is in error by more than 2 minutes (3 minutes or more in NAT HLA)
src.note: This corrected-estimate report applies specifically when not in radar contact; the 3-minute figure is the NAT HLA exception to the general 2-minute rule.

q: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: Enroute in domestic US airspace on CPDLC, you want to send Center a free-text message explaining a ride-smoothing request. Is free text available to you here?
a: No. When operating with CPDLC, free text is only supported in oceanic airspace; in domestic airspace free text is not supported and you must use standard aviation terminology only.

src.ref: FOM 7.1.2.1, Common Language and Standard Phraseology
src.quote: text is only supported in oceanic airspace. Only use standard aviation terminology. Free text in domestic airspace is not supported.
src.note: Domestic CPDLC is limited to standard terminology; free text is an oceanic-only capability.

q: CHECK AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are inbound IFR to a non-towered airport and self-announcing your position on CTAF. What three elements must each position report contain?
a: Company ID and type of aircraft; position and altitude; and direction of flight and intentions (landing or overflying).

src.quote: Position reports should include: • Company ID and type A/C • Position and Altitude • Direction of flight and intentions (landing or overflying)
src.note: Position reports are announced at points such as the IAF, 10 miles or FAF inbound on CTAF, downwind, base, final, and clearing the runway.

q: In the US terminal area, must the A330 add "Heavy" to its call sign?
a: Yes. The 787 and A330 must add the word "Heavy" to the call sign in all air/ground communications in the terminal area. It is not required during enroute communications.

src.quote: The 787 and A330 aircraft must add the word “Heavy” to the aircraft’s call sign (e.g., “Alaska Twenty-one Heavy”) in all air/ground communications in the terminal area. The term “Heavy” is not required during enroute communications.
src.note: Outside the US, Heavy applies to aircraft with takeoff weights of 300,000 lbs or more and is only required on initial contact with tower and approach/departure control.

q: On the A330, how does the Flight Crew alert the Flight Attendants to an emergency, and how do the Flight Attendants alert the Flight Crew?
a: Flight Deck to cabin: press the EMER button. Cabin to Flight Deck: press the PRIO CAPT button once.

src.quote: (A330) pressing the PRIO CAPT button once.
src.note: The Flight Deck to cabin line reads: (A321/A330) pressing the EMER button. The PM then immediately attempts interphone communication with the Flight Attendants.

q: Name a new trigger in Rev 125 for calling Ops after landing.
a: When directed by 10-7 guidance.

src.quote: Directed by 10-7 guidance.
src.note: Other listed triggers include medical assistance needed at the gate and through-jumpseaters on the Freighter.

q: Where are safety reports filed, and what topics does the single system cover?
a: In the Safety Reporting System, accessed on the EFB app or by a link on the Pilot web page. It covers fatigue, ASAP, hazards, issues, concerns, occurrences, incidents, irregularities, and accidents.

src.quote: Safety reports can be filed in the Safety Reporting System, which can be accessed on the EFB app or by a link on the Pilot web page. Safety reports include items such as fatigue, ASAP, other hazards, issues, concerns, occurrences, incidents, irregularities, and accidents.
src.note: Rev 125 consolidated reporting into one system.

q: At what moment is an Alaska Airlines flight considered dispatched (the Point of Dispatch)?
a: When an OUT time is generated.

src.ref: FOM 8.1.1, Types of Operations Authorized for Dispatch
src.quote: A flight is considered dispatched at the Point of Dispatch, which occurs when an OUT time is generated.
src.note: Flight Dispatch releases and dispatches aircraft under Domestic or Flag rules as appropriate; the OUT time is the regulatory trigger, not brake release or takeoff.

q: When a flight is dispatched under Exemption 11047 without a destination alternate, what runway conditions must exist at the destination at the ETA?
a: Two separate usable runways at the estimated time of arrival, with at least one usable runway having an operational instrument approach procedure.

src.quote: At least one of the usable runways has an operational instrument approach procedure.
src.note: Exemption 11047 also requires the Dispatcher to add the statement 'FLT RELEASED UNDER EXEMPTION 11047' to the Dispatch Release.

q: Using the Derived Alternate Airport IFR Weather Minimums table, what additives apply when an airport has only ONE operational navigational facility (single straight-in non-precision, CAT I, or circling)?
a: Add 400 ft to the MDA(H) or DA(H) as applicable, and add 1 sm (or 1600 m) to the landing minimum.

src.ref: FOM 8.2.2.1, Destination Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
src.quote: Add 400 ft to MDA(H) or Add 1 sm or 1600 m to A CAT I precision approach procedure, DA(H), as applicable landing minimum
src.note: Table 8.2.2.1 cells run together in the text extract. Read as: one operational navigational facility, add 400 ft to MDA(H) or DA(H) as applicable, and add 1 sm or 1600 m to the landing minimum.

q: What alternate-minimums additives apply when an airport has at least TWO operational navigational facilities serving different suitable runways?
a: Add 200 ft to the higher DA(H) or MDA(H) of the two approaches used, and add 1/2 sm (or 800 m) to the higher authorized landing minimum.

src.ref: FOM 8.2.2.1, Destination Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
src.quote: At least two operational navigational Add 200 ft to higher Add 1/2 sm or 800 m facilities, each providing a straight-in DA(H) or MDA(H) to higher authorized
src.note: Table 8.2.2.1 cells run together in the text extract. Read as: at least two operational navigational facilities to different suitable runways, add 200 ft to the higher DA(H) or MDA(H) of the two approaches used, and add 1/2 sm or 800 m to the higher authorized landing minimum.

q: Per 14 CFR 121.621, when is a destination alternate always required for a Flag flight regardless of destination weather?
a: Any Flag flight planned for more than six hours flight time as calculated on the Flight Plan requires a destination alternate.

src.ref: FOM 8.2.2.1, Destination Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
src.quote: an alternate is required for any Flag flight more than six hours flight time as planned on the Flight Plan
src.note: The same 6-hour rule is repeated in 8.2.3 for the no-alternate cases to/from Alaska and international locations under A012.

q: How does Alaska define 'marginal' for the alternate airport when deciding whether a second alternate is required?
a: The alternate is marginal when either its ceiling OR visibility is at alternate minimums (as derived from the Alternate Airport IFR Weather Minimums table).

src.quote: Alternate airport weather is considered marginal when either the ceiling OR visibility is at alternate minimums
src.note: 121.619(a) requires a second alternate when both destination and first alternate are forecast marginal; destination is marginal when ceiling and/or visibility is at or below CAT I minimums.

q: What two change indicators does Exemption 20108 define as 'conditional language' in a TAF or METAR?
a: TEMPO and PROB.

src.quote: The term “conditional language” refers to the change indicators TEMPO and PROB.
src.note: Exemption 20108 lets a Domestic flight dispatch when conditional language shows destination and/or first alternate may go below minimums at ETA.

q: When a flight is dispatched under Exemption 20108, what alternate requirement always applies?
a: A second alternate airport must always be listed on the Dispatch Release.

src.quote: a second alternate airport must always be listed on the Dispatch Release
src.note: Exemption 20108 is not authorized for flag operations or for flights to international destinations operated under Domestic regulations, and requires the release statement 'FLT RELEASED UNDER EXEMPTION 20108.'

q: Within the contiguous 48 states (or Hawaiian Islands), what destination weather allows dispatch with no alternate?
a: Forecasts/reports indicate that at the estimated time of arrival, plus or minus one hour, conditions will be at least a 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility.

src.quote: conditions will be at least 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility
src.note: This is the classic 1-2-3 no-alternate rule: within +/- 1 hour of ETA, 2000 ft ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility.

q: For a no-alternate dispatch to a State of Alaska destination, what runway physical criteria must the airport meet?
a: More than one operational runway with two separate and distinct surfaces (four runway ends), hard-surface with appropriate weight-bearing capability, minimum 100 ft wide, and at least 5500 ft of usable length.

src.quote: minimum of 100 ft wide, and at least 5500 ft of usable length
src.note: Alaska destinations also need 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm (or 2 sm more than lowest applicable minimums, whichever is greater) at ETA +/- 1 hour.

q: For a Flag no-alternate dispatch (14 CFR 121.621(a)) with a straight-in approach available, what ceiling is required from one hour before to one hour after ETA?
a: At least 1500 ft above the lowest published instrument approach minimum, or 2000 ft above airport elevation, whichever is higher (plus 3 miles visibility or 2 miles more than the applicable minimum, whichever is greater).

src.quote: 1500 ft above the lowest published instrument approach minimum or 2000 ft above airport elevation, whichever is higher
src.note: If a circling approach is required instead, the ceiling must be 1500 ft above the lowest circling MDA.

q: For a no-alternate dispatch to Canada under A012, what is the FAF altitude used for most YVR (Vancouver) approaches?

src.quote: FAF altitude for most YVR approaches is 3000 ft.
src.note: The Canada no-alternate criteria require a forecast ceiling at least 1000 ft above the FAF altitude with 3 miles visibility, OR 2000 ft ceiling and 6 miles, plus no thunderstorm or freezing precipitation risk.

q: For passenger operations, how does the ARFF/ICAO index requirement at the destination differ from the requirement at an alternate?
a: At the destination, passenger operations are permitted with an ARFF Index/ICAO category one level lower than that associated with the aircraft (e.g., an Index C aircraft may operate at an Index B airport). For an alternate, a minimum designation of ARFF Index A / ICAO category 4 is required.

src.ref: FOM 8.3.10.2, Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting Requirements (ARFF)
src.quote: For alternates, a minimum designation of ARFF Index A/ICAO 4 is required.
src.note: A difference of more than one ARFF level at the destination requires DO approval before operating into or out of that airport; if ARFF is unavailable at the alternate's planned arrival time, Dispatch should notify airport management as soon as possible when diverting.

q: Under Domestic fuel rules (14 CFR 121.639), how much reserve fuel is required beyond flying to the destination and most distant alternate?
a: Enough to fly 45 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate after the most distant alternate; with no alternate, 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate.

src.quote: With no alternate, fly for 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate.
src.note: Domestic: destination + most distant alternate + 45 min, or destination + 55 min if no alternate is required.

q: Under Flag fuel rules (14 CFR 121.645), what are the required fuel components?
a: Destination, then 10% of the total time from departure to destination, then the most distant alternate (if required), then 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination or alternate.

src.quote: Fly for 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination airport or alternate
src.note: The 10% burn is on the total departure-to-destination time; the 30-minute hold is at 1500 ft, distinguishing Flag from Domestic reserves.

q: Under the B043 Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations, how are the two extra reserve components computed?
a: 10% of the planned time in oceanic/remote continental airspace, plus 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption (calculated at the flight's weight and altitude at top of descent).

src.ref: FOM 8.3.2.3, Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations (737/787/A321/A330)
src.quote: Fly for a period of 10% of the planned time in oceanic/remote continental airspace
src.note: On the (787/A321/A330) international release these appear as "10% RSV" and "45@CRZ" (B043) versus "30@1500" for standard flag. Rev 125 removed the Hawaii-only restriction.

q: How far before pushback should the Flight Crew contact Dispatch with any changes to desired departure fuel, and who has final say on fuel?
a: At least 30 minutes prior to pushback; if agreement cannot be reached, the Captain has the final decision for fuel on board.

src.quote: the Flight Crew should contact Dispatch at least 30 minutes prior to pushback
src.note: Additional fuel above planned requires agreement of both Captain and Dispatcher before fueling begins; the Captain holds the final decision.

q: What is the maximum flight duration for which an aircraft may be dispatched with all autopilot systems inoperative, and what approval is needed?
a: No aircraft may be dispatched for flights greater than 3.5 hours with all autopilots inoperative without approval from both the Captain and Dispatcher.

src.quote: Aircraft will not be dispatched for flights greater than 3.5 hours if all autopilot systems are inoperative without approval from the Captain and Dispatcher.
src.note: Beyond 3.5 hours all-autopilots-inop requires joint Captain and Dispatcher approval.

q: What is the maximum steady-state wind velocity for takeoff and landing, and which wind value is used for dispatch crosswind computations?
a: 50 kts maximum steady-state wind velocity; steady-state wind velocity is used for crosswind computations for dispatch.

src.quote: Maximum steady-state wind velocity for takeoff and landing is 50 kts
src.note: Operations with a steady-state component near crosswind limits combined with higher gusts should be considered unacceptable; specific limit values are in fleet-specific manuals.

q: For a flight with 1 hour or more of flight time, what weather product controls dispatch/prior to departure per the Weather Required for Dispatch table?
a: The TAF controls (METAR is not controlling) for flight times of 1 hour or more; for flight times under 1 hour both METAR and TAF apply.

src.ref: FOM 8.4.1.4, Weather Required for Dispatch or Amending Destination Enroute
src.quote: TAF (METAR not controlling)
src.note: Enroute and possibly changing destination always requires both METAR & TAF regardless of flight time. Extended overwater Flag flights under ETOPS have a special allowance.

q: When dispatching to an international or military airport that is missing ceiling, visibility, or present weather in the METAR, what TAF conditions and alternate planning are required?
a: The TAF must indicate at least a 1000 ft ceiling and 3 miles visibility from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA, two alternates with complete METAR and TAF must be planned, and the MDA is limited to 1000 ft AGL.

src.ref: FOM 8.4.2.3, Missing Weather at International and Military Airports
src.quote: The TAF indicates the weather conditions from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA will be no less than a ceiling of 1000 ft and visibility of 3 miles.
src.note: No circle-to-land is permitted with missing ceiling/visibility, and departures are prohibited if freezing precipitation is forecast with missing weather elements.

q: Planned redispatch is authorized under which type of operations, and why is it used?
a: Flag operations only; it is an FAA-authorized procedure used to minimize the fuel required to meet the 10% flag fuel requirement.

src.quote: Dispatching with a plan to redispatch while enroute (planned redispatch) is an FAA-authorized procedure used in flag operations to minimize the amount of fuel required to meet the 10% fuel requirement.
src.note: The redispatch waypoint must be common to both routes and specified on the original release; within two hours but no later than 20 minutes prior to the waypoint the destination alternate may be removed if the intended destination meets no-alternate requirements.

q: Check-airman scenario: You dispatch an A330 on a domestic leg with a destination alternate required, and later the same day the crew flies an international flag leg. Contrast the required reserve fuel components for the domestic leg versus the flag leg.
a: Domestic (14 CFR 121.639): fuel to the destination, then to the most distant alternate, plus 45 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate, or 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate if no alternate is required. Flag (14 CFR 121.645): fuel to the destination, then 10% of the total departure-to-destination time, then to the most distant alternate if one is required, then 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination or alternate.

src.quote: Fly for a period of 10% of the total time required to fly from the departure airport to and land at the destination airport, then
src.note: Domestic keys on the 45/55-minute last-cruise-rate reserve; Flag adds the 10%-of-total-time burn plus a 30-minute hold at 1500 ft, the signature that separates the two.

q: Check-airman scenario: You have pushed and are taxiing out when Dispatch needs to change your alternate and add required fuel. Does this require a release amendment, and what makes the amendment valid?
a: Yes. An alternate change and a required-fuel change are each on the release-amendment list, so the Dispatcher must forward an amended release. The Captain acknowledges acceptance by verbally accepting via Company communications, by acknowledging an ACARS message containing the amended information, or by leaving a signed copy at stations that require paper. At the time of amendment all dispatch rules (14 CFR 121.593 through 121.661 and 121.173) must be met.

src.quote: If it becomes necessary for the PIC or Dispatcher to change the conditions of the release, the Dispatcher shall forward an amended release.
src.note: Alternate change and Required Fuel change both appear on the (AS) release-amendment list (8.5.1.4). Any airborne change to destination or alternate also requires a recalculated Flight Plan/Dispatch Release with associated weather and NOTAM information.

q: Check-airman scenario: You are planning an A330 from SEA to LAX, both in the contiguous 48. The LAX forecast at ETA +/- 1 hour is 2500 ft ceiling and 4 sm. May you dispatch with no destination alternate, and what is the governing rule?
a: Yes. Within the contiguous 48 states (or the Hawaiian Islands), no alternate is required if forecasts or reports indicate that at ETA +/- one hour conditions will be at least a 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility. 2500 and 4 clears the 1-2-3 threshold. An alternate is still required for any Flag flight planned more than 6 hours, and one must be listed if thunderstorms or volcanic ash are forecast in the TAF at the ETA.

src.quote: conditions will be at least 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm
src.note: The 1-2-3 rule: within +/- 1 hour of ETA, 2000 ft ceiling and 3 sm. Thunderstorms or volcanic ash forecast in the TAF at the ETA still force an alternate onto the release.

q: Check-airman scenario: An A330 is dispatched from the West Coast to Hawaii under planned redispatch, with the redispatch waypoint set late in the overwater leg. How late may Dispatch remove the destination alternate, and what condition must the intended destination meet?
a: Within two hours of arrival at the redispatch point, but no later than 20 minutes prior to the redispatch waypoint, the destination alternate may be removed from the redispatch Flight Plan, provided the intended destination meets the no-alternate requirements. Planned redispatch is authorized in flag operations only, and the redispatch waypoint must be specified on the original release and common to both routes.

src.quote: Within two hours, but no later than 20 minutes prior to the redispatch waypoint, the destination alternate may be removed from the redispatch Flight Plan, provided the intended destination meets the no alternate requirements.
src.note: Redispatch exists to minimize the 10% flag fuel. Planned-redispatch flights to/from Hawaii must depart with an alternate for the intended destination (8.2.3). If routing is modified to bypass the redispatch point, redispatch stays valid without further planning within 100 nm of the planned route (8.5.9.1).

q: Rev 125: how far before scheduled departure is the Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan made available, and which A330 flying is the exception?
a: 90 minutes as standard. Exceptions: Interisland Hawaii 70 minutes; South Korea departures 180 minutes; Amazon Cargo 180 minutes; and, new in Rev 125, (787/A330) Europe departures 180 minutes.

src.quote: A Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan will be generated and made available to the Flight Crew 90 minutes prior to the scheduled flight departure time except as noted below: • Interisland Hawaii: 70 minutes • South Korea Departures: 180 minutes • Amazon Cargo: 180 minutes • (787/A330) Europe Departures: 180 minutes
src.note: The (787/A330) Europe line is new in Rev 125, and it drives a D-180 Operational Control Window per FOM 2.2.2.1.

q: On an HA international A330 release, how much may the actual takeoff weight exceed the PTOW before the Flight Plan is no longer valid?
a: The Flight Plan is still valid as long as the ATOW is no more than 3000 lbs greater than the PTOW. More than 3000 lbs over requires a revised Dispatch Release.

src.quote: The Flight Plan is still considered valid as long as the ATOW is no more than 3000 lbs greater than the PTOW.
src.note: Between PTOW and 3000 lbs over, adjust MIN T/O and MIN RLS by the per-1000-lb figure printed on the release. The legend was rebuilt in Rev 125 on an A330 example.

q: When must Dispatch perform a landing performance analysis for contamination, and what must it cover?
a: When any contamination is anticipated at the destination or alternate. It should cover both the anticipated and the worst acceptable braking action for the planned landing weight.

src.quote: This analysis should cover both the anticipated and worst acceptable braking action for the planned landing weight.
src.note: Rev 125 broadened the trigger. The Dispatcher and Captain should brief runway conditions before departure when braking action is anticipated less than good and landing performance is critical.

q: On the A330 international release, how do the B043 reserves appear in the fuel summary compared with standard flag?
a: B043 shows "10% RSV" and "45@CRZ"; standard flag shows "10% RSV" and "30@1500".

src.ref: FOM 8.3.2.3, Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations (737/787/A321/A330)
src.quote: (787/A321/A330) The B043 Dispatch Release is the same as the international Dispatch Release, except for the 45 minute and 10% fuel quantities listed in the fuel summary.
src.note: Ops Spec B043: 10% of planned time in oceanic/remote continental airspace plus 45 minutes at normal cruise consumption at top-of-descent weight and altitude.

q: In the 8.1.3 Authorized Airports table, which designations may be planned as an adequate airport, and what does the asterisk mean?
a: Any airport designated A, F, R, P, or E may be planned as an adequate airport, provided the 6.2.1 criteria are met and it is within the approved area of operations. The asterisk means it may be used as an ETOPS alternate unless restricted by F&F or Company NOTAM.

src.quote: May be used as an ETOPS alternate unless restricted by F&F or Company NOTAM. Adequate Airports Any airport designated in this table as A, F, R, P, or E may be planned as an adequate airport (to define ETOPS entry and exit points) for all Alaska Airlines fleets provided the adequate airport criteria from 6.2.1 – Adequate Airport is met and the airport is within the approved area of operations for the aircraft being operated, unless restricted by F&F or Company NOTAM.
src.note: Rev 125 replaced the per-fleet lists with one table carrying 717/737/787/A321/A330 columns.

q: Per the (AS) definition, when is a runway classified as a Wet Runway?
a: When more than 25% of the runway area being used is visibly damp or covered by no more than 1/8 inch (3 mm) of water, slush, dry snow, or wet snow.

src.quote: More than 25% of the runway area (length and width) being used is visibly damp or covered by no more than 1/8 inch (3 mm) of water, slush, dry snow, or wet snow.
src.note: The 25% coverage plus 1/8 inch (3 mm) threshold is the dividing line; beyond 1/8 inch of loose contaminant the runway becomes Contaminated.

q: In the absence of a descriptor, at what temperatures are snow considered dry versus wet?
a: Snow is considered dry at temperatures -3 degrees C or colder, and wet at temperatures -2 degrees C or warmer.

src.quote: snow is considered dry at temperatures -3°C or colder
src.note: Dry snow can be blown if loose or will not stick together to form a snowball; wet snow makes a well-compacted snowball but water will not squeeze out.

q: What does a Slippery When Wet NOTAM tell the crew about the runway condition code?
a: It is a continuous alert that if the runway were to become wet, it would immediately degrade to 3/3/3 instead of 5/5/5.

src.quote: degrade to 3/3/3 instead of 5/5/5.
src.note: Usually caused by rubber deposits; the reduced braking applies when the runway is in fact wet, and the NOTAM remains visible even when the runway is dry.

q: May a braking action PIREP be used to upgrade the expected braking action from the RCAM or FICON?
a: No. A PIREP may only downgrade expected braking action; it must not be used to upgrade it, and airport personnel cannot issue braking action reports.

src.quote: A PIREP must not be used to upgrade the expected braking action.
src.note: A PIREP from a similar size aircraft may be used when no FICON is available or to downgrade expected braking action.

q: Is reduced thrust using assumed temperature (AT or FLEX) authorized on a contaminated runway?
a: No. Reduced thrust using assumed temperature, labeled AT or FLEX, is not authorized on a contaminated runway.

src.ref: FOM 9.1.8, Takeoff Operations on a Wet/Contaminated Runway
src.quote: Reduced thrust using assumed temperature, labeled AT or FLEX, is not authorized on a contaminated runway.
src.note: Takeoff data selection depends on whether the contaminant is hard-packed (accelerate-stop concern) or loose (also a drag concern after engine failure).

q: When landing on a smooth runway in moderate or heavy rain, what RWYCC must the crew plan with, and when may RWYCC 5 be used?
a: Consider the surface contaminated with standing water and use data associated with a RWYCC of 2. RWYCC 5 may be used with light rain (-RA) on any runway, or on a SK-R runway with moderate rain (RA).

src.quote: must use landing performance data associated with a RWYCC of 2 when planning to land on
src.note: The RWYCC 2 requirement applies to a smooth runway under moderate (RA) or heavy rain (+RA), or a SK-R runway under +RA.

q: How is the Latest Touchdown Point (LTP) calculated, and when must it be briefed?
a: Subtract landing distance from LDA and add 1000 ft for air-run. Brief LTP when LDA is less than 7000 ft or BA is less than GOOD.

src.quote: Subtract landing distance from LDA and add 1000 ft for air-run.
src.note: LTP calculations are not applicable for Autoland.

q: May WET landing data be used when the Landing Distance Available is less than 7000 ft?
a: No. For LDA less than 7000 ft, do not use WET data.

src.quote: For LDA less than 7000 ft, do not use WET data.
src.note: For LDA less than 7000 ft with BA less than GOOD, the maximum selectable autobrake setting must be used if available.

q: For the A330, what minimum prepared surface width must contaminated runway preparation leave for takeoffs and landings to be allowed?
a: No less than 45 m (148 ft).

src.note: Takeoffs and landings are prohibited if contaminated runway preparation leaves an available prepared surface width less than the A330 figure of 45 m (148 ft). The 787 and A321 share the value; the 717 is 30 m and the 737 is 18 m.

q: At what contaminant depths, and at what contaminated-runway tailwind, are takeoffs prohibited?
a: When contaminant depth is greater than 1/2 inch for wet snow, slush, or water, or greater than 4 inches for dry snow; and when the steady-state tailwind component exceeds 10 kts on a contaminated runway.

src.quote: Contaminant depth is greater than 1/2 inch for wet snow, slush, or water or greater than 4 inches for dry snow.
src.note: A steady-state tailwind component exceeding 10 kts on a contaminated runway also prohibits takeoff.

q: At what steady-state wind velocity are takeoffs and landings prohibited?
a: When steady-state wind velocity is greater than 50 kts.

src.quote: Steady-state wind velocity is greater than 50 kts.
src.note: Takeoffs and landings are also prohibited when braking action is NIL or the RWYCC is 0 on any portion of the runway, and with moderate or greater freezing rain.

q: In heavy snow, what anti-ice fluid and timing are required for takeoff?
a: The aircraft must be anti-iced with undiluted Type IV fluid and a successful Contamination Check completed within 5 minutes of takeoff.

src.quote: successful Contamination Check has been completed within 5 minutes of takeoff
src.note: Type IV is preferred; if not available, Type II may be used.

q: When barometric pressure exceeds 31.00 inches of Hg, what altimeter setting is used for enroute operations below 18,000 ft MSL?
a: Set 31.00 and maintain it until beyond the affected area or reaching the final approach segment; on departure/missed approach set 31.00 prior to a mandatory/crossing altitude or 1500 ft AGL, whichever is lower.

src.quote: Set 31.00 for enroute operations below 18,000 ft MSL.
src.note: Airports unable to accurately measure pressures above 31.00 inHg report 'in excess of 31.00 inches of Hg,' and operations there are limited to VFR weather conditions.

q: How is Moderate airframe icing described, and what action does it require?
a: The rate of accumulation is such that even short encounters become potentially hazardous; use of deicing/anti-icing equipment or flight diversion is necessary.

src.quote: even short encounters become potentially hazardous
src.note: With Severe icing, deicing/anti-icing fails to control the hazard and immediate flight diversion is necessary. Trace and Light become a concern chiefly over 1 hour.

q: How fast does fuel temperature typically move toward TAT, and how fast in extreme conditions?
a: Approximately 3 degrees C per hour typically, but as high as 12 degrees C per hour in extreme conditions.

src.quote: at a rate of approximately 3°C per hour but can be as high as 12°C per hour in extreme conditions
src.note: To warm fuel, a 4000 ft descent below the tropopause yields about a 7 C TAT increase, and an increase of M 0.01 produces about a 0.7 C TAT increase; in severe cases descent as low as 25,000 ft may be needed.

q: When temperature is colder than ISA, how does true altitude compare to indicated altitude?
a: True altitude is lower than indicated altitude.

src.quote: true altitude is lower than indicated altitude
src.note: This effect becomes extremely important with very cold temperatures and minimum terrain separation; US charts note in the briefing strip when cold temperature corrections apply.

q: What is the policy on intentionally operating through validated severe or extreme turbulence?
a: Under no circumstances will a flight be operated intentionally through areas of validated severe or extreme turbulence.

src.quote: Under no circumstances, will a flight be operated intentionally through areas of validated severe or extreme turbulence.
src.note: Avoidance of departure/arrival routings is not required for moderate clear air turbulence at climb/descent altitudes; it is safer to transit those altitudes as rapidly as practical with cabin precautions.

q: By how much must a thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo be avoided, and how must cloud tops be cleared?
a: Avoid by at least 20 miles. When in the clear on top, clear cloud tops by 5000 ft; if clearing by less than 5000 ft, avoid the thunderstorm by 20 nm.

src.quote: Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo.
src.note: Also avoid flying under a cumulonimbus overhang; if unavoidable, use antenna up tilt to locate and avoid hail.

q: What restriction applies below 1000 ft AGL when ATC has reported a Microburst Alert, and how long do windshear/microburst advisories remain in effect?
a: Do not take off or continue an approach below 1000 ft AGL to that runway. Windshear and microburst advisories remain in effect for 20 minutes after the alert is issued.

src.quote: Do not take off or continue approach below 1000 ft AGL to a runway where ATC has reported a Microburst Alert.
src.note: Takeoffs and landings are permitted with windshear or microburst advisories in effect, but the crew should exercise caution.

q: How close may a flight operate to a volcano where an eruption is imminent or underway, and above what latitude are flights not dispatched with solar radiation S3 or higher?
a: Not within 10 nm of a volcano with an imminent or underway eruption when significant ash emission is likely; and Alaska will not dispatch flights at latitudes above 78 degrees N with solar radiation S3 or higher.

src.quote: Flights will not operate within 10 nm of a volcano where an eruption is imminent or underway
src.note: Per 9.7.5, radiation is a significant concern at high latitudes; the 78°N / S3 dispatch limit is a hard cutoff. A significant space weather event is R3, S3, or G4 or greater.

q: Check-airman scenario: You are departing on a runway with a FICON of 3/3/3, packed snow, a hard-packed contaminant. Your FO wants to use a FLEX (assumed temperature) takeoff. What thrust setting is legal here, and why does contaminant type drive your data selection?
a: Reduced thrust using assumed temperature (AT/FLEX) is NOT authorized on a contaminated runway, stop your FO before they select it. Takeoff data selection is based on contaminant type: hard-packed is an accelerate-and-stop concern, while loose contaminant also requires concern for drag when continuing takeoff after an engine failure. Use the appropriate contaminated-runway data at full/rated thrust.

src.ref: FOM 9.1.8, Takeoff Operations on a Wet/Contaminated Runway
src.quote: Reduced thrust using assumed temperature, labeled AT or FLEX, is not authorized on a contaminated runway.
src.note: Takeoff data selection is based on the type of contaminant, hard-packed or loose. Hard-packed contaminant is an accelerate-and-stop concern, while loose contaminant also requires concern for drag when continuing takeoff after an engine failure.

q: Check-airman scenario: Night approach into a mountainous field at -40°C, and the chart briefing strip flags cold-temperature corrections. A new FO on IOE asks whether the jet is really where the altimeter reads. What do you tell them about true versus indicated altitude, and when does the error bite hardest?
a: When temperature is colder than ISA, true altitude is LOWER than indicated altitude, the airplane is physically lower than the altimeter shows. The effect becomes extremely important with very cold temperatures and minimum terrain separation, which is exactly why US instrument approach charts flag the correction in the briefing strip. Apply the published cold-temperature altitude corrections.

src.quote: When the temperature is lower than International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), true altitude is lower than indicated altitude.
src.note: This temperature effect on indicated altitude becomes extremely important with very cold temperatures and minimum terrain separation; within the US, instrument approach charts contain a note in the briefing strip when cold temperature corrections are to be applied.

q: Check-airman scenario: Cruising at night you paint a cell giving an intense radar echo about 15 miles off the nose. You're tempted to press on and overfly it in the clear on top. What lateral and vertical clearances does the FOM require, and is 15 miles enough?
a: Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo, 15 miles is inside the limit, so deviate. When 'in the clear' on top, cloud tops should be cleared by 5000 ft; if you can only clear the tops by less than 5000 ft, you must avoid the storm by 20 nm. Also avoid flying under a cumulonimbus overhang.

src.quote: Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo.
src.note: When 'in the clear' on top, cloud tops should be cleared by 5000 ft. If clearing the cloud tops by less than 5000 ft, avoid the thunderstorm by 20 nm.

q: Check-airman scenario: On short final at 900 ft AGL, the tower calls a Microburst Alert for your landing runway; the alert was issued 8 minutes ago. May you continue the approach, and how long does that advisory bind you?
a: No, do not continue an approach below 1000 ft AGL to a runway where ATC has reported a Microburst Alert. At 900 ft AGL you are already below the gate, so go around. Windshear and microburst advisories remain in effect for 20 minutes after issuance, so an 8-minute-old alert is still active; hold, wait it out, or divert.

src.quote: Do not take off or continue approach below 1000 ft AGL to a runway where ATC has reported a Microburst Alert.
src.note: Windshear and microburst advisories remain in effect for 20 minutes after the alert has been issued. Takeoffs and landings are permitted with windshear or microburst advisories in effect; however, the Flight Crew should exercise caution.

q: In what unit do ICAO SNOWTAMs report contaminant depth, and what must the crew do with it?
a: Millimeters. Convert to inches for AS policy adherence (1/8 in is 3.175 mm, 1/4 in is 6.35 mm, 1/2 in is 12.7 mm, 1 in is 25.4 mm).

src.quote: Note that contaminant depth is reported in millimeters, and will need to be converted to inches for AS policy adherence.
src.note: New in Rev 125 with a conversion table. ICAO airports may report RCAM data using the term GRF (Global Reporting Format).

q: How does Alaska Airlines define a significant space weather event for dispatch purposes?
a: Radio Blackout R3 or greater, Solar Radiation S3 or greater, or Geomagnetic storm G4 or greater.

src.quote: significant space weather events are defined by Alaska Airlines as Radio Blackout R3 or greater, Solar Radiation S3 or greater, or Geomagnetic storms G4 or greater.
src.note: Rev 125 changed the definition. Flights are not dispatched above 78 degrees N with solar radiation S3 or higher (9.6.1).

q: Where does the A330 crew find landing performance data for a reported RWYCC?
a: In the FCOM, In-Flight Performance.

src.quote: • (A330) See FCOM – In-Flight Performance
src.note: The RCAM generates the RWYCC for runways in use; the A330 performance data lives in the FCOM In-Flight Performance section.

q: Where is CRM placed in Alaska Airlines' CRM/TEM model, and what does that placement signify?
a: CRM is intentionally placed at the bottom of the model to signify that CRM is the foundation of TEM.

src.ref: FOM 10.1, Alaska Airlines CRM and TEM
src.quote: Crew Resource Management (CRM) is intentionally placed at the bottom of the model to signify that CRM is the foundation of TEM.
src.note: The model is built with CRM underneath TEM. Effective TEM depends on the crew's underlying CRM skills.

q: What are the four core CRM skills each Alaska Airlines pilot is expected to maintain and improve?
a: Communication, Workload Management, Leadership, and Flight Discipline.

src.ref: FOM 10.1, Alaska Airlines CRM and TEM
src.quote: a set of core skills (Communication, Workload Management, Leadership, and Flight Discipline)
src.note: These four core skills, plus supportive behaviors, are the framework every pilot is expected to refine over their career.

q: Within the assertiveness ladder (Ask, Say, Command, Assume Control), when should a pilot Assume Control of the aircraft?
a: As a last resort, when safety is at imminent risk due to PF confusion, incapacitation, or inaction.

src.quote: As a last resort, take control of the aircraft when safety is at imminent risk due to PF confusion, incapacitation, or inaction.
src.note: Assume Control is the top rung of the Ask/Say/Command/Assume Control assertiveness ladder and is reserved for imminent risk.

q: What should crew briefings include regarding threats?
a: A review of relevant threats and management strategies to reduce the risk of those threats to the operation.

src.quote: Briefings should include a review of relevant threats and management strategies to reduce the risk of those threats to the operation.
src.note: Briefings should also include specific PM duties when appropriate, and are conducted to the level of detail appropriate to the circumstances.

q: Under Prioritize Tasks in Workload Management, what is the first priority?
a: Fly the aircraft first; when the aircraft is stable and safe, navigate while properly analyzing the situation.

src.quote: Fly the aircraft first.
src.note: Operational tasks are prioritized by risk/criticality to safety of flight, with high-priority tasks accomplished first.

q: How does the FOM direct use of the autopilot in areas of high-density traffic?
a: Use the autopilot as much as practical during operations in areas of high-density traffic.

src.quote: Use the autopilot as much as practical during operations in areas of high-density traffic.
src.note: Automation should be used to prevent excessive workload, and disengaged when it excessively increases workload or reduces situational awareness.

q: Under Address Conflicts, what three forms may a resolution take?
a: Command ("my way"), collaborate ("our way"), or accommodate ("your way").

src.quote: Resolutions may consist of command (“my way”), collaborate (“our way”), or accommodate (“your way”).
src.note: Crews should focus on what is right, not who is right; operational conflicts are resolved as they arise while interpersonal conflicts are resolved as time permits.

q: Under Flight Discipline, what verbal tool does the PM use to restore degraded situational awareness or safety margins?
a: "Ask, Say, Command" as applicable.

src.quote: Uses “Ask, Say, Command” as applicable to restore degraded situational awareness and/or safety margins.
src.note: The PM is primarily responsible for monitoring the aircraft's flight path and assessing/communicating threats within a shared mental model.

q: Into what two categories are threats divided in Alaska's TEM model, and what are examples of each?
a: Environmental threats (outside the airline's direct control, such as weather, ATC, and Terrain) and airline threats (originating within flight operations, such as system malfunctions, scheduling, and ground problems).

src.quote: environmental threats, which are outside the airline’s direct control, such as weather, ATC, and Terrain, and airline threats, which originate within flight operations, such as system malfunctions, scheduling, and ground problems.
src.note: Threats are events, errors, or circumstances that increase operational complexity and require crew attention if safety margins are to be maintained.

q: Into what three types can Flight Crew errors be divided?
a: Aircraft handling, procedural, and communication errors.

src.quote: Flight Crew errors can be divided into three types: aircraft handling, procedural, and communication errors.
src.note: Errors are crew actions or inactions that deviate from intentions/expectations and reduce safety margins; they may be a slip/lapse or induced by a threat.

q: How is an Undesired Aircraft State (UAS) defined?
a: A position, speed, attitude, or configuration of an aircraft that clearly reduces safety margins resulting from Flight Crew error, actions, or inaction.

src.quote: a position, speed, attitude, or configuration of an aircraft that clearly reduces safety margins
src.note: A UAS is a safety-compromising state resulting from ineffective error management; examples include unstable approaches and improper configuration.

q: In the Prevent/Trap/Mitigate framework, what is described as the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors?
a: A threat-based briefing/TPC.

src.quote: A threat-based briefing/TPC is the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors.
src.note: Trapping uses resources like checklists and SOPs; mitigating uses timely resources such as a PM with assertive communication skills once a UAS exists.

q: What three concepts sit at the top of the TEM model and yield successful threat and error management?
a: Anticipate, Recognize, and Recover.

src.ref: FOM 10.1.2.2, Threat and Error Management Philosophy
src.quote: three concepts that yield successful threat and error management: Anticipate, Recognize, and Recover
src.note: These are crewmember habits and skills that must be employed to effectively manage threats and errors.

q: Anticipation is described as a two-step process. What are the two steps?
a: (1) Identify relevant threats, and (2) develop management strategies for each using various resources.

src.quote: It is essentially a two-step process: (1) identify relevant threats and (2) develop management strategies for each
src.note: The PF develops, communicates, and executes the plan; the PM aids by identifying/managing threats and maintaining a shared mental model.

q: In the Recognize phase, what should the PM do if they observe a new threat or error the PF does not respond to?
a: Communicate in a clear, concise, and effective manner what they observed, the "See it, Say it" principle (e.g., PM: "You're 10 knots fast" or "SPEED;" PF: "Correcting").

src.quote: communicate in a clear, concise, and effective manner what they have observed (i.e., “See it, Say it”).
src.note: Communicating this way obligates the PF to respond, improving situational awareness and regaining an adequate margin of safety.

q: SCENARIO, TEM in action: You are briefing an approach into a station where LLWS (low-level windshear) advisories are in effect. Per the Prevent stage of the TEM model, what is your single best resource, and what should the briefing cover?
a: A threat-based briefing/TPC is the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors. With LLWS advisories active, the briefing should review the resources that will keep that threat from progressing into an error or UAS, for example, delay, change runways, adjust speeds, monitor radar, and review windshear procedures.

src.quote: A threat-based briefing/TPC is the best resource for preventing threats from becoming errors. For example, if LLWS advisories are in effect, the briefing should review resources that will be used to prevent that threat from progressing into an error or UAS (e.g., delay, change runways, adjust speeds, monitor radar, review windshear procedures).
src.note: Prevent is the first stage of the Prevent/Trap/Mitigate progression: applying appropriate resources to relevant threats is the most effective way to keep a threat from progressing through the model.

q: SCENARIO, Assertive callout to a senior captain: You are the PM flying with a check airman on the glideslope. The approach is deteriorating and you feel yourself wanting to soften the call because of the captain's seniority. What does the FOM require of your speech in this high-risk moment?
a: Do not mitigate your speech. It is imperative that pilots do not lessen or downplay the importance of a callout in high-risk situations, say it clearly and with the urgency the situation demands, regardless of the other pilot's seniority.

src.quote: It is imperative that pilots do not mitigate their speech (lessen or downplay the importance) in high-risk situations.
src.note: This CAUTION reinforces the assertiveness ladder and the "See it, Say it" principle; seniority does not reduce the PM's obligation to speak up assertively.

q: SCENARIO, Recover, last resort: On approach the aircraft reaches full-scale glideslope deflection. You command "Go around" and the PF does not react. What is the FOM's last-resort action, and what is the exact control-transfer exchange?
a: As a last resort, the PM must assume aircraft control to restore safety margins. The exchange is PM: "I have control, going around." PF: "You have control."

src.quote: As a last resort, the PM must assume aircraft control to restore safety margins. (e.g., PM: “I have control, going around.” PF: “You have control.”).
src.note: This is the top rung of the assertiveness ladder (Assume Control) meeting the top of the TEM model (Recover); it follows an unheeded one- or two-word corrective command.

q: On a two-way radio failure, what transponder code do you select?
a: Change the transponder to code 7600.

src.ref: FOM 11.1.4, Lost Communications – Two-Way Radio Failure
src.quote: If two-way radio failure occurs, change transponder code to 7600.
src.note: If the failure is in or later meets VFR conditions, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable; if in IFR, fly the Route/Altitude/Leave-Clearance-Limit rules of 14 CFR 91.185.

q: If you lose two-way radio and must enter the US ADIZ, what do you do and what code do you squawk?
