a: Use emergency authority and enter the ADIZ as close to the Flight Plan crossing position and time as possible, squawking 7700; then follow standard comm-failure procedures.

src.ref: FOM 11.1.4.1, Entering ADIZ without Radio Contact
src.quote: use emergency authority and enter the ADIZ as close to the Flight Plan crossing position and time as possible with transponder code 7700
src.note: Note the distinction: 7600 for the comm failure itself, but 7700 specifically to enter the ADIZ under emergency authority.

q: What temperature threshold makes an ill traveler a reportable communicable-disease case?
a: A temperature of 100 degrees F (38 degrees C) or greater that has persisted more than 48 hours (or fever with certain other symptoms, or diarrhea).

src.quote: has a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or greater which has persisted more than 48 hours
src.note: Contact MedLink and ensure Dispatch is notified; if the CDC quarantines the aircraft they may direct you to one of the 20 stations on the listed map.

q: Post-decompression, if oxygen needs exceed available masks or quantity, what descent target relieves adverse physiological reactions?
a: After terrain and fuel considerations, a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude should eliminate adverse physiological reactions.

src.quote: a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude, after terrain and fuel considerations are addressed, should eliminate any adverse physiological reactions
src.note: Enroute use or depletion of a POB imposes no restriction on flight operations and requires no pilot action.

q: What is the MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance phone number?

src.quote: MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance may be reached at (602) 282-4910
src.note: On the A330 (and A321), when the Flight Crew calls MedLink they relay information between the cabin and MedLink.

q: After extinguishing a lithium battery fire, why must you cool the device and how long can it take?
a: HALON extinguishes the fire but the device must then be cooled, preferably with water; it may take 15 or more minutes to fully cool. Avoid ice, which insulates and can let remaining cells reignite.

src.quote: It may take 15 or more minutes to completely cool the device.
src.note: AVOID USING ICE to cool the device; ice acts as an insulator, and an insulated but not-yet-cooled device can reignite.

q: Can water be used on a lithium battery fire?
a: Water may be used to fight a lithium ion battery fire, but should not be used on a lithium metal battery fire. Cool with water preferably, or any non-alcoholic liquid if water is not available.

src.quote: Water may be used to fight a lithium ion battery fire, but should not be used on a lithium metal battery fire.
src.note: FIGHT THE FIRE with a HALON extinguisher, then COOL THE DEVICE; non-alcoholic liquids such as milk, fruit juice, or POG are acceptable coolants.

q: What does emergency authority allow the Captain to do in a situation requiring immediate decision and action?
a: Take any action considered necessary, including deviating from prescribed procedures, methods, weather minimums, and regulations to the extent required in the interest of safety.

src.quote: the Captain may take any action considered necessary, including deviating from prescribed procedures, methods, weather minimums, and regulations to the extent required in the interest of safety
src.note: Emergency authority is granted to both the Captain and the Dispatcher; FOM 11.2.1 cites 14 CFR 91.3, 121.557, 121.559, 121.627, and Ops Spec A008.

q: Must you declare an emergency with ATC to use emergency authority?
a: No. The Captain may use emergency authority without declaring an emergency if traffic or handling priority is not needed, but should still advise ATC of intentions as soon as possible.

src.quote: The Captain may use emergency authority without declaring an emergency with ATC if traffic or handling priority is not needed.
src.note: The FOM adds: do not hesitate to declare an emergency if the situation warrants it.

q: Name situations the FOM says pilots will consider an emergency.
a: Fire or smoke endangering the aircraft; inability to definitely establish position; failure of a component jeopardizing safety of flight; an in-flight medical condition requiring a diversion; and a high probability of an emergency evacuation.

src.quote: An in-flight medical condition that requires a diversion
src.note: Immediately advise ATC and Dispatch; if workload is high or time short, ask ATC to notify the Company.

q: When should MAYDAY be used versus PAN-PAN?
a: MAYDAY (said three times) is the distress signal reserved for life-threatening situations; PAN-PAN (said three times) is the urgency signal for urgent situations that are not immediately life-threatening but require assistance.

src.ref: FOM 11.2.2.1, Distress and Urgency Communication Signals
src.quote: Mayday should be reserved for life-threatening situations.
src.note: Pan-Pan is for urgent situations that are not immediately life-threatening but require assistance from someone on the ground.

q: What information belongs in an emergency message, and what is the Alaska HAZMAT emergency contact number?
a: Nature of emergency; number of passengers/crew and infants; passengers needing special assistance and their location; the HAZMAT emergency contact number if hazardous cargo is aboard (AS: 206-392-6465); and fuel remaining in minutes.

src.quote: If there is hazardous cargo on board, relay the HAZMAT emergency contact number:
src.note: The (AS) HAZMAT number is 206-392-6465; report fuel remaining in minutes.

q: After exercising emergency authority that deviates from FARs or company procedures, by when must a Captain file the safety report?
a: As soon as possible, but no later than the conclusion of the next mandatory 24-hour rest period. A Dispatcher who exercises emergency authority must report within 10 days.

src.quote: no later than the conclusion of the next mandatory 24-hour rest period
src.note: If the FAA later requests a written report and the crewmember fails to submit one, they may face punitive action including certificate action.

q: Is a minimum fuel advisory an emergency, and when should it be declared?
a: No, minimum fuel is not an emergency and does not imply a need for traffic priority; it should only be declared once the flight has committed to land at a specific airport, not while a divert option still exists.

src.quote: Minimum fuel is not an emergency situation, but merely indicates an emergency situation is possible should any undue delay occur.
src.note: Coordinate any divert decision with Dispatch before declaring; avoid ending up at an alternate with less than 30 minutes of fuel.

q: What must the PIC declare when landing will occur with less than a 30-minute fuel supply, and how is that 30 minutes defined?
a: Declare MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL to ensure priority handling. The 30-minute supply is based on holding fuel flow or higher at 1500 ft above field elevation, and 30 minutes is a minimum the PIC may increase.

src.quote: the PIC shall declare, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL” to ensure priority handling
src.note: The PIC must take every precaution to avoid landing with less than a 30-minute supply, based on holding fuel flow at 1500 ft above field elevation.

q: On a two-engine aircraft flying with one engine inoperative, what factors justify flying beyond the nearest suitable airport?
a: None. Sufficient fuel to fly farther, passenger accommodation other than safety, and availability of maintenance/repair are all specifically not sufficient justification to pass the nearest suitable airport.

src.quote: none of the following factors should be considered sufficient justification to fly beyond the nearest suitable airport
src.note: After an in-flight engine shutdown, land at the nearest suitable airport based on time considerations where a safe landing can be made (FOM 11.2.7).

q: How quickly are quick-don oxygen masks designed to be donned in an emergency descent?
a: With one hand within 5 seconds, because flight crews have very limited time of useful consciousness at altitude.

src.quote: Quick-don masks are designed to be donned with one hand within 5 seconds.
src.note: An emergency descent may be driven by loss of pressurization or other events such as fire or a cabin security incident.

q: For an A330 decompression over charted terrain polygons, what is the initial descent altitude?
a: Always 17,000 ft or FL170 on the A330 (and 737). Only the 787 takes a polygon-specific altitude from the detail drawer in Jeppesen FD Pro.

src.quote: (737/A330) Initial descent altitude is always 17,000 ft or FL170.
src.note: Rev 125 rewrote 11.2.9 and deleted the regional decompression procedures from the theater chapters. Each polygon still has its own escape procedure in the FD Pro detail drawer.

q: What is the NTSB flight attendant briefing format, and what drives whether it is a normal or emergency landing?
a: N - Nature of the emergency, T - Time to prepare, S - Special instructions, B - Brace signal. The type of landing is based on the likelihood of evacuation, not on what is declared with ATC.

src.ref: FOM 11.2.11, Abnormal/Emergency Briefing of Flight Attendants – NTSB
src.quote: The type of landing should be based on the likelihood of evacuation and not what is declared with ATC.
src.note: NORMAL LANDING means no evacuation prep required; EMERGENCY LANDING means evacuation is possible and the cabin should prepare.

q: When may the Cabin Crew initiate an evacuation on their own, and what memory aid lists the triggers?
a: If life-threatening conditions require immediate evacuation and they cannot communicate with the Captain after trying all reasonable means. The FAST acronym lists triggers: Flight Deck incapacitated, Aircraft impacted/at a peculiar angle, Smoke and fire present, Threat of imminent danger.

src.quote: Examples of Cabin Crew-initiated evacuation include (FAST acronym):
src.note: Flight Attendants are separately authorized to initiate an evacuation without Captain orders in an obvious life-threatening situation (FOM 11.2.12).

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You've been holding for weather and it's now apparent you'll touch down with less than a 30-minute fuel supply. What exact call do you make, and how is that 30 minutes defined?
a: Declare "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL" to ensure priority handling. The 30-minute supply is based on holding fuel flow or higher, as required by configuration, at 1500 ft above field elevation; 30 minutes is a minimum the PIC may increase for runway-availability and go-around contingencies.

src.quote: When it becomes apparent that landing will occur with less than a 30-minute supply of fuel, the PIC shall declare, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL” to ensure priority handling.
src.note: Do not confuse this with minimum fuel (11.2.5), which is not an emergency and grants no traffic priority.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Rapid decompression at cruise over charted high-terrain polygons in your A330. Walk me through the masks, the descent target that relieves physiological reactions, and how you pick the initial descent altitude.
a: Don quick-don masks (one hand, within 5 seconds), execute the escape procedure for the polygon you are in from the detail drawer in Jeppesen FD Pro, and descend to the initial descent altitude, which on the A330 is always 17,000 ft or FL170. Do not enter another polygon below the altitude indicated in the polygon detail drawer unless terrain clearance is assured. After terrain and fuel are addressed, a descent to 8000 ft cabin altitude should eliminate adverse physiological reactions.

src.quote: Do not enter another polygon while navigating at less than the altitude indicated in the polygon detail drawer unless terrain clearance is assured.
src.note: Rev 125.1. (737/A330) initial descent altitude is always 17,000 ft or FL170; only 787 altitudes vary by polygon. Quick-don masks are designed to be donned with one hand within 5 seconds (11.2.8).

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A passenger collapses two hours into an overwater leg. Who do you contact, who has final authority on whether to divert, and how does the A330 crew loop the flight attendants into the call?
a: Contact MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance at (602) 282-4910; with MedLink's advice and Dispatch, the Captain determines whether a medical diversion is necessary and coordinates diversion-airport preferences. Company policy is to follow MedLink's recommendation, but the Captain retains final authority on any operational request. On the A330 the Flight Crew relays information between the cabin and MedLink.

src.quote: the Captain will determine whether a medical diversion is necessary and coordinate with Dispatch and MedLink for diversion airport preferences.
src.note: MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance: (602) 282-4910. (A321/A330) The Flight Crew will relay info between cabin and MedLink (11.1.9.3).

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You shut an engine down in flight. A field 20 minutes closer has a shorter runway; your maintenance base is 90 minutes ahead with plenty of fuel to reach it. Where do you land, and does the extra fuel or the maintenance base justify pressing on?
a: Land at the nearest suitable airport, based on time considerations, where a safe landing can be made. On a two-engine aircraft with one engine inoperative, neither sufficient fuel to fly farther, nor passenger accommodation other than safety, nor availability of maintenance/repair justifies flying beyond the nearest suitable airport.

src.quote: If an engine fails or is shut down in flight, land the aircraft at the nearest suitable airport, based on time considerations, where a safe landing can be made.
src.note: Per 11.2.7.1, none of these justify passing the nearest suitable airport: extra fuel, passenger accommodation other than safety, or maintenance/repair availability.

q: On the A330, how long after engine shutdown do the DFDR and CVR stop recording?
a: 5 minutes after engine shutdown (A321/A330/A330F).

src.ref: FOM 11.2.14, Cockpit Voice Recorder and Digital Flight Data Recorder
src.quote: (A321/A330/A330F) DFDR/CVR will stop recording 5 minutes after engine shutdown.
src.note: After an incident or accident the recorders must be preserved; on the 717/737 the crew pulls the CVR and DFDR circuit breakers.

q: What is the purpose of the decompression polygon procedures?
a: They provide a calculated safe method for descending to 10,000 ft before passenger oxygen supplies are depleted following a rapid decompression over high terrain.

src.quote: Decompression polygon procedures provide a calculated safe method for descending to 10,000 ft before passenger oxygen supplies are depleted following a rapid decompression over high terrain.
src.note: Rewritten in Rev 125. The PIC is expected and encouraged to exercise sound judgment; weather, visibility, ATC and grid MORAs may also inform the course of action.

q: Fueling with passengers boarding, on board, or deplaning at the gate is permitted only if certain cabin conditions are met. Name the required states of the Seat Belt Sign and the No Smoking Sign, and one other required condition.
a: The Seat Belt Sign is off and the No Smoking Sign is on. Other required conditions include: all engines shut down, aircraft chocked, a jetbridge/airstairs/boarding ramp at the door, the primary passenger entry door open, electrical power and lights on, and minimum Flight Attendants stationed near a continuously open floor-level exit.

src.quote: Fueling/Defueling/Fuel transferring is permitted while passengers are boarding, remaining on board, or deplaning provided
src.note: The full provided list also requires chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, primary door open, power and lights, Seat Belt Sign off, and No Smoking Sign on.

q: During gate fueling with passengers on board, who is responsible for confirming fueling is complete, and at what point?
a: The Captain verifies fueling is complete prior to door closure.

src.quote: The Captain verifies fueling is complete prior to door closure.
src.note: This is a Captain-specific verification captured in the Note under the at-gate fueling conditions.

q: When fueling with passengers on board away from the gate area (no loading bridge or adequate stairs), what power source and door conditions are required?
a: The APU or GPU must be available, all engines shut down, all doors armed, communications available with the fueler for the duration of fueling, and F/As stationed at their assigned exits keeping the slide deployment areas clear.

src.quote: APU or GPU must be available.
src.note: Communication with the fueler may be by radio, headset, or voice through the First Officer's window, and F/As must be notified when fueling begins and ends.

q: Under what circumstance may an aircraft be fueled with one engine running, and what happens if fleet-specific procedures do not cover it?
a: Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air would result in a stranded aircraft, per the FH/FCOM procedures. If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, fueling with one engine running is not authorized.

src.ref: FOM 12.1.1.3, Fueling with One Engine Running
src.quote: If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, then fueling with one engine running is not authorized.
src.note: Normally all engines are shut down during fueling; the single-engine-running case is an exception tied to avoiding a stranded aircraft.

q: In a fuel spill with passengers on board, who decides whether to deplane, and on which side of the aircraft are passengers deplaned?
a: The Pilot-In-Command decides whether to deplane (if no pilot is on board, the 'A' Flight Attendant/FFA decides). If there is a choice of exits, passengers are deplaned on the side of the aircraft opposite the fuel spill.

src.quote: passengers will be deplaned on the side of the aircraft opposite the fuel spill.
src.note: Any ground air conditioning unit should also be terminated to prevent pushing fumes into the aircraft and to remove an ignition source.

q: If fueling is required from a non-Alaska Airlines approved fuel vendor, what must be done before fueling begins?
a: Contact Maintenance Control before fueling begins; Maintenance Control provides the Captain with the required fuel acceptance procedures.

src.quote: contact Maintenance Control before fueling begins.
src.note: The Captain does not self-clear a non-approved vendor; Maintenance Control supplies the acceptance procedures.

q: Before operating the aircraft, what are the two acceptable states for every circuit breaker, and how is the 'normal position' identified visually?
a: Every circuit breaker shall be either in the normal position or properly pulled. In the normal position the CB is snapped into the closed position and the white stem is not visible.

src.quote: The CB is snapped into the closed position. The white stem is not visible.
src.note: Company-standard collars for pulled CBs are fluorescent yellow or red, though a different color collar does not affect airworthiness.

q: During a maintenance engine run at the gate, what is the power limit and what flap configuration is required?
a: Engines shall not be operated above idle power at a gate, and flaps shall remain retracted during the maintenance run.

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1, Maintenance Engine Run at Gate (CAUTION)
src.quote: Engines shall not be operated above idle power at a gate. Flaps shall remain retracted during the maintenance run.
src.note: Pilots are never authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance, defined as any thrust setting above idle.

q: May passengers be on board during a maintenance-run pressurization check, and is fueling permitted during engine runs with passengers aboard?
a: No. Passengers shall not be on board during a pressurization check, and fueling operations during engine runs are prohibited with passengers on board, deplaning, or loading.

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1.1, Passengers, F/As, and Doors – Passenger Aircraft (WARNING)
src.quote: Passengers shall not be on board during a pressurization check.
src.note: Ramp activity should not be allowed behind an operating engine, and engine runs for an air contamination event or pressurization check are done without passengers/F/As on board.

q: On the A330, what restriction applies to a #1 engine run relative to the boarding door and jetway?
a: #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s).

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1.2, Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft
src.quote: (787/A330) #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s).
src.note: Doors not used for boarding are also closed to minimize the FOD hazard, both pilots are at their stations, and the aircraft is chocked with the parking brake set.

q: Are pilots ever authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance, and how is 'high power' defined?
a: No. Pilots are not authorized to conduct high power engine runs for maintenance at any time. High power engine runs are defined as any engine thrust setting above idle.

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1.2, Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft (Note)
src.quote: High power engine runs are defined as any engine thrust setting above idle.
src.note: At the completion of the maintenance idle engine run, the crew completes the Shutdown/Parking Checklist.

q: With a yellow-side MSP-1 displayed on the power/thrust levers, may the aircraft be operated for flight, and what activities are still allowed?
a: No. With the yellow side displayed the aircraft may not be operated for the purpose of flight, but preflight may be performed (including normal Flight Deck flows and checklists, fueling, passenger boarding, etc.). Verbal permission from Maintenance in lieu of the logbook or yellow MSP-1 is not authorized.

src.quote: The aircraft may not be operated for the purpose of flight, but preflight may be performed
src.note: The Flight Crew installs the MSP-1 yellow side out whenever there is an open discrepancy in the logbook.

q: If the MSP-1 card is not installed and the logbook is not in the Flight Deck, how is the aircraft's status treated?
a: The aircraft status is treated as if the card were installed with the RED side up until the logbook is returned to the Flight Deck (i.e., systems/controls cannot be operated by non-Maintenance personnel).

src.quote: the aircraft status will be treated as if the card were installed with the RED side up until the logbook is returned to the Flight Deck.
src.note: The red side warns that safety-sensitive maintenance is being performed and non-Maintenance personnel may not operate systems or controls.

q: If an aircraft is designated Out of Service and the ACARS OTS message is received, what must occur before pushback even if the defect has been signed off?
a: Dispatch must be contacted prior to pushback even if the defect resolution has been signed off and the aircraft has been released.

src.quote: If the ACARS OTS message is received, Dispatch must be contacted prior to pushback even if the defect resolution has been signed off and the aircraft has been released.
src.note: The OTS designation auto-generates an ACARS message to the aircraft and Dispatch when the Load Closeout is sent.

q: For the A330, a high-speed rejected takeoff requires a Maintenance Logbook entry above what speed, and what three items must be noted?
a: Above 100 kts (Airbus). Note the gross weight, reject speed, and braking effort.

src.quote: • Rejected takeoff – high speed above (Airbus) 100 kts/(Boeing) 80 kts (note gross weight, reject speed, braking effort)
src.note: This is one of many mandatory logbook entries, alongside limitation exceedances, hard/overweight landings, and returns for landing due to mechanical reasons.

q: For an HA aircraft, on what time reference is the MEL valid period based, and may an aircraft depart with an MEL that will expire during the flight?
a: For HA, the MEL valid period is based on GMT, and an aircraft may not depart a station with an MEL whose time limit will expire during the planned duration of the flight.

src.quote: An aircraft may not depart a station with an MEL whose time limit will expire during the planned duration of the flight.
src.note: By contrast, the AS valid period is based on Seattle local time and a flight may be dispatched if departure is within the valid period even if it ends outside it.

q: For a non-ETOPS HA flight, how long is the Overnight Check valid in flight hours and in clock hours?
a: The Overnight Check is valid for 25 flight hours in service and must not exceed 48 consecutive clock hours. A Post Flight Check does not reset the 48-hour Overnight Check requirement.

src.quote: The Overnight Check is valid for 25 flight hours in service and must not exceed 48 consecutive clock hours.
src.note: The PIC must verify the Airworthiness Release was signed off in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook prior to each non-ETOPS flight or group of flights.

q: May an aircraft depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook, and what entry must Maintenance make at major maintenance airports for open entries?
a: No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook. At major maintenance airports, Maintenance must make a balancing entry in the 'Action Taken' or 'Correction/Deferral' column for all open entries.

src.quote: No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook.
src.note: Under the Crew Placarding Procedure the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete the balancing entry to return the aircraft to service.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You're the Captain at the gate, passengers boarding, fuel truck pumping. Your new First Officer, wanting to reduce cabin glare, reaches up and turns the No Smoking Sign OFF while leaving the Seat Belt Sign ON, and fueling continues. What is wrong, and what are the correct sign states plus the exit condition you must confirm?
a: The FO has both signs backwards. Fueling with passengers requires SONO: Seat Belt Sign OFF, No Smoking Sign ON. He must reverse both. You must also confirm chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, the primary door open, power and lights, and minimum Flight Attendants stationed near a floor-level exit that remains continuously open as the deplaning route.

src.quote: Fueling/Defueling/Fuel transferring is permitted while passengers are boarding, remaining on board, or deplaning provided
src.note: The provided list requires the Seat Belt Sign off and the No Smoking Sign on (SONO), plus chocks, all engines shut down, a bridge/stairs/ramp at the door, primary door open, power and lights, and an FA at a continuously open floor-level exit.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Maintenance requests a #1 engine idle run at the gate to troubleshoot. The jetway is still extended to the forward boarding door, which is open with two agents aboard. May you start the #1 engine, and what must change first?
a: No. On the A330, #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s). Retract the jetway and close that door first. Doors not used for boarding are closed to minimize FOD, both pilots must be at their stations, the aircraft chocked with parking brake set, and a dedicated Engine Safety Observer stationed at the side of the engine.

src.ref: FOM 12.3.1.2, Procedure and Safety Requirements – All aircraft
src.quote: #1 engine runs are not permitted with the boarding door(s) open or the jetway extended to the boarding door(s).
src.note: Doors not used for boarding are closed to minimize the FOD hazard; both pilots at their stations, aircraft chocked, parking brake set, dedicated Engine Safety Observer at the engine.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: At a remote station your APU is MEL'd inoperative, there is no ground power and no ground air, and you will be stranded if you shut down. Ground crew asks if you can hot-fuel with the #2 engine running. Assume the A330 fleet-specific manuals publish no procedure for single-engine-running fueling. Are you authorized?
a: No. Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air would strand the aircraft, and only per the FH/FCOM procedure. If the fleet-specific manuals do not specify a procedure, fueling with one engine running is not authorized regardless of the stranding risk.

src.ref: FOM 12.1.1.3, Fueling with One Engine Running
src.quote: If procedures are not specified in fleet-specific manuals, then fueling with one engine running is not authorized.
src.note: Fueling with one engine running is only considered where a lack of APU, external power, or ground air will result in a stranded aircraft, per the FH/FCOM.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: After block-in at an outstation with no HA maintenance, you write up a discrepancy. Maintenance Control says the item is deferrable and directs you via ACARS to make a balancing entry to return the aircraft to service. The outbound Captain sees an open write-up with nothing in the 'Action Taken/Correction/Deferral' column. May the aircraft depart as-is, and who may direct the balancing entry?
a: No aircraft may depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook. At major maintenance airports Maintenance makes the balancing entry in the 'Action Taken' or 'Correction/Deferral' column for all open entries. When authorized under the Crew Placarding Procedure, the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete that column to return the aircraft to service.

src.quote: No aircraft will be allowed to depart with an open maintenance discrepancy in the logbook.
src.note: At major maintenance airports Maintenance makes a balancing entry in the Action Taken or Correction/Deferral column; under the Crew Placarding Procedure the MOC may direct the Flight Crew to complete it.

q: Who may remove a yellow-side MSP-1 from the power/thrust levers, and under what condition may the Flight Crew do it?
a: Maintenance, or the Flight Crew after they verify with Maintenance and confirm a clean logbook is on board the aircraft.

src.quote: An MSP-1 on the yellow side can be removed by Maintenance or by the Flight Crew after they verify with Maintenance and confirm a clean logbook is on board the aircraft.
src.note: Rev 125 added the Flight Crew removal path.

q: When correcting a minor error in the Maintenance Logbook, what identification does an HA pilot write next to the correction?
a: Initials and (HA) Employee ID (AS pilots use their PeopleSoft number). Draw a single line through the mistake; never erase or white out.

src.quote: Correct minor errors by drawing a single line through the mistake and writing your initials and (AS) PeopleSoft number or (HA) Employee ID next to the correction.
src.note: Major errors are corrected by voiding the (AS) page or (HA) block.

q: When must Flight Attendants verify the suitability of exit seat customers?
a: Prior to each door closure, to ensure each customer meets exit seat criteria.

src.quote: must verify suitability of exit seat customers prior to each door closure
src.note: Verification is repeated before every door closure, not just at initial boarding, so re-boarded or reseated passengers are re-checked.

q: Who has final authority in determining suitability of exit seat occupants?
a: The Flight Attendants, in accordance with FAA regulations.

src.quote: Flight Attendants have final authority in determining suitability criteria of exit seat occupants on board the aircraft
src.note: A CRO may be consulted for an exit seat disability concern, but the FA retains final say on exit-seat suitability.

q: If a CRO does not deny boarding, can the PIC still override that decision?
a: Yes. The PIC has authority to override the CRO's decision based on a safety-of-flight concern.

src.quote: If a CRO does not deny boarding, the PIC has the authority to override the decision based on a safety-of-flight concern.
src.note: The CRO manages ACAA compliance, but safety of flight keeps the PIC as the final decision-maker on carriage.

q: When ACAA compliance conflicts with an FAA regulation, which takes precedence?
a: FAA regulations take precedence.

src.quote: if ACAA compliance conflicts with FAA regulation, FAA regulations take precedence
src.note: A CRO may waive Company policy to mitigate a disability, but cannot waive an FAA regulation.

q: How does the FOM define a service animal?
a: A dog, regardless of breed or type, that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a qualified individual with a disability.

src.quote: A service animal is defined as a dog, regardless of breed or type, that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks
src.note: The disability covered may be physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability.

q: After an in-flight unacceptable service animal incident, what should the Flight Crew relay?
a: Seat number, passenger name, a brief description of the incident, and a request that a CRO meet the aircraft.

src.quote: Request that a CRO meet the aircraft
src.note: At the gate the FAs instead consult a CRO before departure per 13.3.1; the four-item relay applies after departure.

q: May spare lithium batteries be placed in checked baggage?
a: No. Spare lithium batteries may not be placed in checked baggage due to the potential fire hazard; they must go in carry-on baggage.

src.quote: Spare lithium batteries of any type, including external battery chargers containing a lithium- ion battery, may not be placed in checked baggage because of the potential fire hazard.
src.note: Checked baggage may only contain lithium batteries installed in a device; spares must be carried on with terminals covered/insulated.

q: When may passengers use cell phone transmit (talk/text) features during a ground delay?
a: During a ground delay of 15 minutes or longer, with the Captain's permission.

src.quote: during a ground delay of 15 minutes or longer with the Captain’s permission.
src.note: Transmit features are also allowed until door closure and while taxiing to the gate on arrival; the Captain may suspend use at any time if interference is suspected.

q: Which mobility-device batteries may be carried and stowed in the passenger cabin?
a: Only lithium-ion batteries used to power mobility devices; all other mobility device batteries must be stowed in the cargo compartment.

src.quote: Only lithium-ion batteries used to power mobility devices can be carried and stowed in the passenger cabin.
src.note: A NOTOC is not required for these batteries; wet-cell (spillable) and gel/dry-cell batteries go in the cargo compartment.

q: What will the Flight Deck Report state when a lithium-ion wheelchair battery is carried in the cabin?
a: The Flight Deck Report will state "Lithium Battery Wheelchair," and the "A" FA/FFA notifies the Captain of the battery's location.

src.quote: the Flight Deck Report will state “Lithium Battery Wheelchair.”
src.note: Wheelchairs with lithium-ion batteries that cannot be easily removed will not be transported; the removed battery rides in the cabin.

q: Are Portable Oxygen Concentrators (POCs) considered HAZMAT?
a: No. Authorized POCs are not considered HAZMAT and may be carried in the cabin and used by passengers.

src.quote: POCs are not considered HAZMAT
src.note: An authorized POC is on the FAA-approved list or bears a red-lettered label stating it meets FAA-acceptance criteria.

q: How must filled oxygen bottles be transported, and what documents are required?
a: In an approved container (superbox), shipped as HAZMAT; a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required.

src.quote: filled oxygen bottles must be transported in an approved container (superbox) and are shipped as HAZMAT; therefore, a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required
src.note: Empty oxygen bottles are not HAZMAT and require no superbox or NOTOC; a DOT Special Permit allows filled bottles without a superbox within Alaska to remote communities.

q: How does the crew handle a DNR request to withhold resuscitation on board?
a: Cabin crews are obligated to perform resuscitation attempts; any request to withhold must be denied unless otherwise instructed by MedLink.

src.quote: any request to withhold resuscitation attempts must be denied unless otherwise instructed by MedLink
src.note: Alaska cannot validate a DNR order in flight, but will not refuse travel to a DNR customer if escort/other requirements are met.

q: In an apparent death on board, until when is the individual presumed alive?
a: The individual is presumed alive until MedLink or a physician has determined that death has occurred.

src.quote: The individual is presumed to be alive until MedLink or a physician has determined that death has occurred.
src.note: MedLink assumes liability for stopping CPR; radio communication to indicate a death occurred on board is inappropriate.

q: Under the Fallen Soldier Program, how are the family and military escort boarded and deplaned?
a: "Last On" during boarding and "First Off" during deplaning; the military escort is seated in first class if available.

src.quote: The family and military escort should be “Last On” during boarding and “First Off” during deplaning.
src.note: The remains normally load into an aft pit; keep the Seat Belt Sign illuminated until after the escort and family have deplaned (13.14.3.2).

q: SCENARIO: On the A330, a customer seated in the emergency exit row raises a disability concern moments before door closure. The gate agent already checked him in and a CRO, called to consult, believes the seat is fine. The lead Flight Attendant judges the customer cannot perform the exit functions. Who has the final say on whether he keeps that exit seat, and on what basis?
a: The Flight Attendant. Per FOM 13.1, Flight Attendants have final authority in determining suitability of exit seat occupants on board the aircraft, in accordance with FAA regulations. A CRO may be called to consult on an exit-seat disability concern, but the FA decides the exit seat and must verify suitability prior to each door closure.

src.quote: If an exit seat “disability concern” is expressed by a customer, a CRO may be called to consult with Flight Attendants on how to address the situation in accordance with the Air Carrier Access Act. Flight Attendants have final authority in determining suitability criteria of exit seat occupants on board the aircraft in accordance with FAA regulations.
src.note: Verification is required prior to each door closure. If the customer is reseated after door closure and is continuing past the next stop on the same aircraft, the FAs must inform the pilots to notify the station.

q: SCENARIO: Your A330 is airborne. A passenger's service animal, a dog, growls and lunges at other customers in the cabin, meeting the unacceptable-behavior criteria. There is no CRO on board. As Flight Crew, what four items should you relay so the situation is handled on arrival?
a: Relay the seat number, the passenger name, a brief description of the incident, and a request that a CRO meet the aircraft (FOM 13.3.2, After Departure). At the gate before departure the FAs instead consult a CRO per 13.3.1; the four-item relay is the after-departure procedure.

src.quote: After an incident involving unacceptable service animal behavior, the Flight Crew should relay the following: • Seat number • Passenger name • Brief description of the incident • Request that a CRO meet the aircraft
src.note: A service animal is defined in 13.3 as a dog, regardless of breed or type, individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a qualified individual with a disability.

q: SCENARIO: Two oxygen items show up for the same A330 flight. A passenger wants to bring an authorized Portable Oxygen Concentrator (POC) into the cabin and use it in cruise; separately, Cargo presents a filled oxygen bottle for the hold. How is each handled, and what paperwork does the filled bottle require?
a: The authorized POC may be carried in the cabin and used by the passenger, and is NOT considered HAZMAT (FOM 13.7). The filled oxygen bottle must be transported in an approved container (superbox) and is shipped as HAZMAT, so a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required (FOM 13.8.1). Empty bottles are not HAZMAT and need no superbox or NOTOC.

src.ref: FOM 13.7, Portable Oxygen Concentrator (POC); 13.8.1, Oxygen Bottle Transportation
src.quote: Authorized POCs may be carried in the cabin and used by passengers. An authorized POC is either on the FAA-approved list available to the CSA and in the Flight Attendant Manual, or it will have a label in red lettering stating it meets the FAA-acceptance criteria. POCs are not considered HAZMAT.
src.note: An authorized POC is on the FAA-approved list or bears a red-lettered label stating it meets FAA-acceptance criteria. A DOT Special Permit allows filled bottles without a superbox within Alaska to remote communities where ground or vessel transportation is unavailable.

q: May hazardous materials be carried in the flight deck of an Alaska aircraft?
a: No. No hazardous materials may be carried in the flight deck of any aircraft, except excepted items required for operation (e.g., an installed fire extinguisher) or personal HAZMAT allowances.

src.quote: No hazardous materials may be carried in the Flight Deck of any aircraft. This does not apply to excepted items required for operation (e.g., installed fire extinguisher) or personal HAZMAT allowances.
src.note: The prohibition is on the flight deck specifically; installed equipment and personal allowances are carved out.

q: Under what FAA Ops Spec is Alaska Airlines authorized to carry hazardous materials?
a: Ops Spec A055, Carriage of Hazardous Materials (HAZMAT), which certifies the company is authorized by the FAA to accept, handle, and carry HAZMAT.

src.quote: Alaska Airlines is issued FAA Ops Spec A055, Carriage of Hazardous Materials (HAZMAT).
src.note: A055 is the operations specification underpinning all DG carriage; DG are handled per IATA DGR and 49 CFR.

q: Does the PIC handle dangerous goods or carry civil/criminal liability for them?
a: No. The PIC does not handle DG and does not have civil or criminal liability for DG. Acceptance is done by the DG Acceptance Agent via a thorough acceptance checklist.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.2, Dangerous Goods – Acceptance, General Information, and Responsibilities
src.quote: The PIC does not handle DG and does not have civil or criminal liability for DG.
src.note: The Acceptance Agent and a computerized database perform acceptance; the PIC's role is notification and awareness via the NOTOC.

q: What does NOTOC stand for?
a: Notification to Captain. It is the form that prints the DG information the PIC needs to deal with any emergency.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.2, Dangerous Goods – Acceptance, General Information, and Responsibilities
src.quote: printed on a form called a “NOTOC” which stands for Notification to Captain.
src.note: DG regulations require the PIC receive a NOTOC so they have the information needed for emergencies; the Dispatcher also has access to a copy.

q: How many NOTOC copies are printed for an AS flight, and what does the PIC do with them?
a: Two copies are printed, one for Ops and one for the Captain. The Ramp Agent signs both; the PIC signs both, returns one to the RSA/Ramp Lead, and retains the other for the duration of the flight.

src.quote: Two copies of the NOTOC are printed, one for Ops and one for the Captain.
src.note: The Ramp Agent must verify no damaged or leaking packages and sign before presenting the copies to the PIC.

q: On HA, when is the eNOTOC sent to the flight crew relative to departure?
a: Departure time minus 30 minutes for trans-Pacific and international flights, and departure time minus 15 minutes for inter-island flights.

src.quote: sent to the Flight Crew at departure time minus 30 minutes for trans-Pacific and international flights and at departure time minus 15 minutes for inter-island flights.
src.note: The eNOTOC also prints automatically on all aircraft.

q: When may the AS Captain sign the hard-copy NOTOC?
a: Only after the Ramp Agent has signed it. The PIC signs both hard copies to acknowledge awareness of the DG listed.

src.quote: Signing both hard copies of the NOTOC (only after the Ramp Agent has signed it) to acknowledge awareness of the DG listed on the NOTOC.
src.note: The Captain reviews the NOTOC for correct departure airport, flight number, and tail number; hand edits to tail number and DG location are allowed by the Ramp Lead.

q: How does the HA Captain acknowledge the eNOTOC, and are hand edits allowed?
a: By selecting either ACCEPT* on the MCDU or ACKNOWLEDGE NOTOC on the Comm page, depending on fleet type. Hand edits are not permissible on HA.

src.quote: Acknowledging the eNOTOC by selecting either “ACCEPT*” on the MCDU or “ACKNOWLEDGE NOTOC” on the Comm page (depending on fleet type).
src.note: Contrast with AS, where the Ramp Lead may hand-edit the tail number and DG location; on HA hand edits are not permissible.

q: When is a hand-generated (written) NOTOC used on AS?
a: Only when any computer-generated NOTOC is not available, and only for time-critical DG shipments such as medical supplies or AOG parts.

src.quote: used when any computer-generated NOTOC is not available and only for time-critical DG shipments such as medical supplies or AOG parts.
src.note: The normal version is the FOGS NOTOC; the cargo management system NOTOC (hash-marked) is the computer-generated backup.

q: For how many flights is a NOTOC valid on AS?
a: One flight only. A new NOTOC is required for each flight segment, and also whenever a new DG shipment is added after the NOTOC package arrives at the aircraft.

src.quote: Each flight segment (NOTOC valid for one flight only)
src.note: Any new DG added after the package arrives also triggers a new NOTOC.

q: What is the dry ice limit that does not require a NOTOC entry for a passenger, and does it change internationally?
a: Dry ice may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person on domestic flights only. International flights require a NOTOC.

src.quote: Dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person (domestic flights only, international flights require a NOTOC)
src.note: For cargo, the same 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) applies per package under UN1845, domestic only.

q: Which UN numbers cover lithium-ion/lithium metal cells or batteries that (as small Section II batteries) do not require a NOTOC entry?
a: UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells), coded ELI/ELM.

src.quote: UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells) (ELI/ELM)
src.note: These are the small-battery exceptions; larger lithium shipments still require a NOTOC.

q: What crosscheck does the ACARS Load Closeout provide against the NOTOC on AS?
a: The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must equal the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC. It is a discrepancy crosscheck only; if none, the message reads 'No HAZMAT.'

src.quote: The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must be equal to the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC
src.note: The Load Closeout HAZMAT message is informational and not required for dispatch; contact Station Operations for any discrepancy.

q: Whom does the AS PIC contact with concerns about a DG shipment, and when may the PIC reject it?
a: Contact Cargo Network Support at 1-877-815-8254, staffed 24/7. The PIC may reject if the shipment arrives too late to review and sign the NOTOC, or if concerns cannot be resolved with the RSA/Ramp Lead or Air Cargo personnel.

src.quote: contact Cargo Network Support at 1-877-815-8254. Cargo Network Support is staffed 24/7.
src.note: Notify Operations with the reason for rejecting any DG, and time permitting notify the RSA/Ramp Lead.

q: How often is the DOT ERG updated, and which Guide is used when nothing else is available?
a: The DOT ERG is updated every four years. If no UN/ID number, Proper Shipping Name, or placard lookup is available, search Guide 111 and use that guidance until qualified help arrives.

src.quote: search “Guide 111” and use that Emergency Response Guide information until qualified help arrives on scene.
src.note: The DOT ERG is updated every four years and lives on the EFB; the DOT ERG also carries first-aid info the ICAO ERG decode tables do not.

q: What do the packing groups PG I, PG II, and PG III indicate?
a: Relative risk of a substance: PG I High, PG II Medium, PG III Low.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.21, Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS)
src.quote: Relative risk (PG I High; PG II Medium; PG III Low) of a particular substance.
src.note: Packing Group is one of the NOTOC data fields alongside Class/Division and Sub-Risk.

q: On the NOTOC, when is Gross Weight (weight including packaging) used?
a: Gross Weight is only used for Class 9 DG shipments. Otherwise the Quantity field shows Net Weight, excluding packaging.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.21, Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS)
src.quote: of the DG product including packaging. Only used for Class 9 DG shipments.
src.note: Net Weight excludes packaging; Transportation Index (TI) applies to Class 7 Radioactive instead of weight.

q: How are the lower-compartment pit numbers arranged, and are they accessible in flight?
a: Pits 1, 2, 3 are forward and 4, 5, 6 are aft. All DG shipments in the lower compartments on all aircraft are inaccessible in flight.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.21, Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS)
src.quote: Pits 1, 2, 3 are fwd and 4, 5, 6 are aft.
src.note: The NOTOC also notes all lower-compartment DG is inaccessible in flight.

q: What HAZMAT emergency contact numbers may be given to ATC when declaring an emergency with HAZMAT on board?
a: AS: Chief Dispatcher 888-526-4392 or 206-392-6465. HA: Dispatch 1-808-838-5566. Dispatch is responsible for notifying down-line ARFF.

src.quote: (AS) Chief Dispatcher 888-526-4392 or 206-392-6465
src.note: These numbers expedite HAZMAT information on type, location, and quantity to ATC and down-line ARFF.

q: For a gate-checked wheelchair/mobility device battery, what PIC notification is required?
a: No NOTOC is required, but PIC verbal or SSR notification is required. There is no quantity or weight limit, and the battery is processed by the Gate/Ramp Agent.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.25, Dangerous Goods – Exceptions and Variations
src.quote: No NOTOC required. PIC verbal or SSR notification required.
src.note: Spillable batteries are removed and stored in a battery box; lithium-ion may be carried in the cabin if removable per 13.6.

q: During an airborne DG spill/leak producing toxic fumes or smoke, what should the crew consider for protection?
a: Consider supplemental oxygen or PBE use for all crewmembers, notify ATC and Dispatch, relay the HAZMAT emergency number (AS 206-392-6465 / HA 808-838-5566), and consider declaring an in-flight emergency.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.26, Dangerous Goods – Damaged or Leaking (Airborne)
src.quote: consider supplemental oxygen or PBE use for all crewmembers.
src.note: If the spill involves infectious substances, immediately notify the local public health authority.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are Captain on the A330. Your eNOTOC lists three DG shipments, but the ACARS Load Closeout shows four HAZMAT lines. What is this crosscheck telling you and what do you do?
a: On AS the number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must equal the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC. This is a discrepancy crosscheck only; a mismatch means you contact Station Operations to reconcile the load closeout HAZMAT section against the actual HAZMAT status before you rely on the NOTOC. Note the HAZMAT Load Closeout message is informational and not required for dispatch.

src.quote: The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must be equal to the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC (Exception: see Systems Failures below). This is a discrepancy crosscheck only.
src.note: If no HAZMAT is on the flight the Load Closeout reads 'No HAZMAT'; contact Station Operations for any discrepancy.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: At the gate, a passenger's lithium-ion powered wheelchair is being checked at the jet bridge and no NOTOC prints. Does 'no NOTOC' mean nothing is required of you as PIC?
a: No. Gate-checked wheelchair/mobility device batteries require No NOTOC, but PIC verbal or SSR notification is still required. There is no quantity or weight limit and the device is processed by the Gate/Ramp Agent; a lithium-ion battery may be carried in the cabin if it can be removed and the 13.6 requirements are met. Do not let 'no NOTOC' become 'no notification.'

src.ref: FOM 14.1.25, Dangerous Goods – Exceptions and Variations
src.quote: No NOTOC required. PIC verbal or SSR notification required.
src.note: Spillable batteries are removed and stored in a battery box; non-spillable power is disabled and the battery removed if not securely attached.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A passenger boards your A330 with dry ice packing a cooler of fresh fish. On a domestic segment no NOTOC is needed within limits, but when does that dry ice become a NOTOC item?
a: For passenger items, dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person, and that no-NOTOC allowance is domestic flights only; any international flight requires a NOTOC. For cargo, the same 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) limit applies per package under UN1845, domestic shipments only, international requires a NOTOC.

src.quote: Dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person (domestic flights only, international flights require a NOTOC)
src.note: Exceeding the per-person limit, or crossing a border, moves the shipment onto the NOTOC.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Cargo hands you paperwork for a shipment of lithium-ion batteries coded ELI, declared as meeting Section II. Should this appear as a NOTOC entry, and what would change your answer?
a: No. UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091 lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells), coded ELI/ELM, do not require a NOTOC entry. What changes the answer is size: larger lithium shipments that do not meet Section II still require a NOTOC.

src.quote: UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells) (ELI/ELM)
src.note: Section II small-battery exception only; ELI is lithium-ion, ELM is lithium metal.

q: On the A330 eNOTOC, what does the RRR CAT field indicate?
a: The radioactive category (I, II, or III) of a Class 7 shipment.

src.quote: 18. RRR CAT – Radioactive category I, II, or III.
src.note: Rev 125 reworded the radioactive fields of the A330 eNOTOC legend. The Transport Index unit is associated with the carriage of radioactive substances.

q: Who is designated as the In-Flight Security Coordinator (ISC) for each flight?
a: The Pilot-in-Command (PIC) is designated as the ISC for each flight, responsible for the safety and security of the aircraft, guests, and crewmembers.

src.quote: The Pilot-in-Command (PIC) is designated as the ISC for each flight.
src.note: The ISC performs required duties per the applicable security program for the type of flight operated.

q: At what point is security responsibility transferred to the ISC?
a: Once an aircraft door closes, security responsibility is transferred to the ISC.

src.quote: Once an aircraft door closes, security responsibility is transferred to the ISC.
src.note: The ISC must review pertinent security information with the GSC for each flight segment before the transfer.

q: During what period must the Flight Deck Door be closed and locked under the Secure Flight Deck procedure?
a: From pushback (or from engine start if pushback is not required) until the aircraft has been brought to a stop at its final position on the ramp and the engines are shut down.

src.quote: The Flight Deck Door shall be closed and locked from pushback (or from engine start if pushback is not required) until the time the aircraft has been brought to a stop at its final position on the ramp and the engines are shut down.
src.note: Secure Flight Deck procedures are not required during Part 91 operations.

q: During the Secure Flight Deck period, for what four circumstances may the Flight Deck Door be opened?
a: To conduct a contamination check or perform MEL inspection; to allow a crewmember to attend to physiological needs; to deliver or remove meal service items; and with the Captain's specific approval.

src.quote: To conduct a contamination check or perform MEL inspection
src.note: The time the door is open shall be kept to a minimum, and all door opening and exiting procedures shall be followed.

q: Who is authorized access to the Flight Deck during Secure Flight Deck time?
a: Access is limited to Alaska Airlines crewmembers, Federal Inspectors, Secret Service, Federal Air Marshals, and those with specific authorization.

src.quote: Access to the Flight Deck during Secure Flight Deck time is limited to Alaska Airlines crewmembers, Federal Inspectors, Secret Service, Federal Air Marshals, and those with specific authorization
src.note: Specific authorization references Flight Deck Jumpseat Access procedures.

q: To how long should crewmembers strive to limit the time the Flight Deck Door is open?
a: Three seconds or less, because the Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open.

src.quote: crewmembers should strive to limit the time the door is open to three seconds or less
src.note: If any threat is perceived while the door is open, any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert others to immediately close it.

q: What must any crewmember shout if a threat is perceived while the Flight Deck Door is open?
a: "Door, Door, Door" to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door.

src.quote: If any threat is perceived while the Flight Deck Door is open, any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door
src.note: Flight Deck Lockdown Procedures (15.3.13) are then followed if necessary.

q: If the Flight Crew receives a keypad activation warning signal, what must they assume?
a: Without any other information from the Flight Attendants, they must assume that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack is in progress in the passenger cabin.

src.quote: they must assume, without any other information from the Flight Attendants, that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack, is in progress in the passenger cabin
src.note: The keypad control device shall not be used for normal entry; entry attempts using the keypad shall be denied by the Flight Crew.

q: What is the minimum number of people that must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed after a crewmember exits?
a: A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.6.7, Flight Deck Door Operations With IPSB
src.quote: A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed
src.note: If a pilot and a jumpseater both need to leave, the “A” Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck.

q: May medical personnel be given access to the Flight Deck?
a: No. Medical personnel shall not be given access to the Flight Deck.

src.quote: Medical personnel shall not be given access to the Flight Deck.
src.note: This applies even when MedLink or onboard medical personnel are assisting with a passenger.

q: May a KCM/CMAP participant whose boarding pass shows SSSS use a KCM/CMAP access point?
a: No. KCM/CMAP participants with a boarding pass showing SSSS are not permitted to use KCM/CMAP access points and must proceed to a standard passenger screening checkpoint.

src.quote: If a KCM/CMAP participant has a boarding pass with SSSS printed on it, the crewmember must proceed to a standard passenger screening checkpoint and undergo screening as directed.
src.note: KCM participants also cannot bring other individuals, pets, or others' personal property through KCM access points.

q: Are uniformed crewmembers subject to the one carry-on plus one personal item limit, and what inspection are all their bags subject to?
a: Uniformed crewmembers, whether assigned to a flight or not, are not subject to the one carry-on bag plus one personal item limitation. All bags are subject to random Explosive Trace Detection (ETD) inspection.

src.quote: Uniformed crewmembers, whether assigned to a flight or not, are not subject to the limitation of one carry-on bag plus one personal item.
src.note: Crewmember baggage is not subject to random hand searches after clearing the x-ray unless an illegal or unexplained item is detected.

q: Who is permitted to carry a firearm on duty, and what personal protection devices are Flight Crew prohibited from carrying?
a: Only a Flight Crewmember authorized as a Federal Flight Deck Officer (FFDO) may carry firearms; otherwise the carriage of firearms or other weapons on duty or on Company property is prohibited. Flight Crew are also prohibited from carrying chemical irritating agents such as pepper spray (Mace).

src.quote: the carriage of firearms or other weapons while on duty or while on Company property is prohibited
src.note: The only exception is a Flight Crewmember authorized as an FFDO.

q: Whose ID does the CSA verify for a Federal Air Marshal team, and must the Flight Crew check FAM ID?
a: The FAM Team Lead provides ID to the CSA and advises of additional team members; the CSA only needs to verify the Team Lead's ID. The Flight Crew need not check ID, but if there is doubt as to identity, contact Dispatch via telephone, not the aircraft radio.

src.quote: The CSA only needs to verify the Team Lead’s ID. The Flight Crew need not check ID; however, if there is doubt as to the identity of the individual, contact Dispatch via telephone. Do not use the aircraft radio.
src.note: Do not transmit any communication regarding the FAM program via the radio.

q: What is the standing rule about taking off with a known passenger disturbance?
a: NEVER take off with a KNOWN passenger disturbance.

src.quote: NEVER take off with a KNOWN passenger disturbance.
src.note: If the situation escalates, consider contacting the local airport police for assistance.

q: How many high risk prisoners are allowed per flight and how many armed LEOs must accompany each?
a: Only one high risk prisoner is allowed per flight unless specifically approved in advance by TSA, and each prisoner must be accompanied by two or more armed LEOs who may not be responsible for any other prisoners.

src.quote: Only one high risk prisoner is allowed per flight, unless specifically approved in advance by TSA.
src.note: For low risk, one LEO may control two low risk prisoners on flights up to four hours; two LEOs are required for up to two low risk prisoners on flights over four hours.

q: Once the Flight Deck Door has been locked down in response to a Level 3 or Level 4 threat, may it be reopened?
a: No. The door shall not be reopened under any circumstances; declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport. During Levels 3 and 4 the Flight Attendants will also lockdown the cabin.

src.quote: Once the Flight Deck Door has been “locked down” in response to a Level 3 or Level 4 threat, the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances
src.note: For a Level 1 or Level 2 event, do not terminate lockdown restrictions until the F/As communicate the threat is resolved.

q: Which transponder code is used for hijacking, and may code 7700 be used during a hijacking?
a: Code 7500 is the unique code used for hijacking. Code 7700 shall not be used during a hijacking; that procedure has been eliminated from the common strategy.

src.quote: Code 7500 is the unique code used for hijacking.
src.note: Per 15.3.15.1, do not use code 7700 during a hijacking; ATC will normally ask for confirmation of a 7500 squawk only once due to concern over possible duress.

q: How many distinct passenger threat levels does Common Strategy identify, and what does each describe?
a: Four passenger threat levels: Level One is disruptive behavior, suspicious or threatening; Level Two is physically abusive behavior; Level Three is life-threatening behavior; and Level Four is attempted breach of the Flight Deck or actual breach.

src.quote: There are four passenger threat levels, developed by government and industry experts
src.note: They help identify the seriousness of suspicious or threatening activity occurring on board an aircraft.

q: After deplaning at a remote location for a credible bomb threat during taxiing, how far must the PIC move passengers and crew?
a: The PIC will direct passengers and crew to move at least 100 yards upwind of the aircraft and initiate a passenger and crew count; the GSC ensures ground personnel are at least 100 yards from the aircraft.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.19.2, Credible IED/Bomb Threat – During Taxiing
src.quote: The PIC will direct the passengers and crew to move at least 100 yards upwind of the aircraft
src.note: An aircraft with a credible bomb threat may never be taxied to the gate until the NOC/SOCC deems the threat terminated.

q: SCENARIO (Flight Deck Door discipline): In cruise, the First Officer opens the Flight Deck Door to step out per the exit procedure. As the door swings open, a passenger near the forward galley suddenly lunges toward the aisle. What is the required immediate action, and what is the door-open time target?
a: Any crewmember who perceives the threat must loudly shout "Door, Door, Door" to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door, then follow Flight Deck Lockdown Procedures (15.3.13) if necessary. Crewmembers strive to keep the door open three seconds or less because the Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open.

src.quote: If any threat is perceived while the Flight Deck Door is open, any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door.
src.note: The Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open, so crewmembers should strive to limit the time the door is open to three seconds or less.

q: SCENARIO (jumpseat / two-person rule): You are the Captain. Your First Officer and the flight-deck jumpseater both need to leave the Flight Deck at the same time. What must occur before both can step out?
a: A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed. Because a pilot and the jumpseater both need to leave, the "A" Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck to hold the number at two. The second person closes and secures the door and follows Flight Deck Reentry Procedures when the crewmember returns.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.6.7 - Flight Deck Door Operations With IPSB
src.quote: If a pilot and the jumpseater both need to leave, the “A” Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck.
src.note: A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed; if a jumpseater remains, the F/A does not need to enter.

q: SCENARIO (threat level response): In cruise you receive a keypad activation warning signal, with no other communication from the Flight Attendants. What must the Flight Crew assume, and once locked down at that level, may the door be reopened?
a: Without any other information from the Flight Attendants, the Flight Crew must assume a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack is in progress in the passenger cabin. Once locked down in response to a Level 3 or Level 4 threat, the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances; declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport.

src.quote: If the Flight Crew receives a keypad activation warning signal they must assume, without any other information from the Flight Attendants, that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack, is in progress in the passenger cabin.
src.note: Per 15.3.13, once locked down for a Level 3 or 4 threat the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances, declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport.

q: SCENARIO (armed LEO notification): Armed Individuals are already continuing through on your aircraft, and additional Armed Individuals are joining for the next segment. What must be completed before the aircraft door(s) can be closed?
a: All notifications must be made to the assigned crew and all Armed Individuals before the door(s) can be closed. The gate agent must inform each AI of the location of the others who are armed, including FAMs, and communications between Flight Crew, Flight Attendants, and AIs should be as discreet as possible.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.8, Armed Individuals (other than FAM and FFDO)
src.quote: If AIs are joining a flight where AIs are continuing through, all notifications must be made to the assigned crew and all AIs before the door(s) can be closed.
src.note: The gate agent must inform the AI of the location of others who are armed, including FAMs; communications should be as discrete as possible.

q: Rev 125: on an aircraft with the IPSB installed, what must happen before the Flight Deck Door is opened during the Secure Flight Deck period?
a: The IPSB must be deployed before the Flight Deck Door is opened. A Secure Flight Deck is the combination of a locked door and, where equipped, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier.

src.quote: A Secure Flight Deck is achieved by using a combination of a locked Flight Deck Door and, for aircraft so equipped, an Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) between the cabin and the Flight Deck for use when the Flight Deck Door must be opened. Any time the Flight Deck Door is opened during the Secure Flight Deck period for aircraft with the IPSB installed, the IPSB shall be deployed before the Flight Deck Door is opened.
src.note: NEW in Rev 125. 15.2.6.6 is now 'Flight Deck Operations Without IPSB' and 15.2.6.7 is 'Flight Deck Door Operations With IPSB'.

q: Rev 125: on the A330, which galley cart arrangement options remain when the Flight Deck Door is opened without an IPSB?
a: Options 1 or 2 only. Rev 125 deleted Option 3 for the 787/A330.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.6.6 - Flight Deck Operations Without IPSB
src.quote: (787/A330) Arrange carts and Cabin Crew in accordance with Options 1 or 2.
src.note: Through 124.2 this read Options 1, 2, or 3. Option 3 no longer exists for the 787/A330. On the 717/737/A321 a second F/A stands facing aft as the cabin observer instead.

q: How many types of NRFO operations does the FOM define, and what are they?
a: Three: (1) Flights that must be operated under Part 121, (2) Flights that may be operated under Part 91, and (3) Flights operated under Part 121 Cargo Only.

src.quote: There are three types of NRFO operations
src.note: NRFOs are all flight operations that are not on the published schedule. The type determines the governing rules and Flight Attendant requirements.

q: What three conditions must be met to operate an NRFO under Part 121?
a: The aircraft is on the Operations Specifications, the aircraft is equipped and maintained per the Alaska Airlines Maintenance Program, and the crew is fully qualified.

src.quote: Aircraft is on the Operations Specifications
src.note: All three conditions must be satisfied before a Part 121 NRFO may be dispatched.

q: Are Flight Attendants required on a cargo-only NRFO?
a: No. Flight Attendants are not required on a cargo-only NRFO.

src.quote: Flight Attendants are not required on a cargo-only NRFO.
src.note: Non-essential passengers are also not allowed on flights dispatched as Part 121 – Cargo Only.

q: On a Part 91 NRFO, at what passenger count is a Flight Attendant required to be on board?
a: A Flight Attendant must be on board if more than nineteen (19) passengers are carried.

src.quote: a Flight Attendant must be on board if more than nineteen (19) passengers are carried
src.note: Alaska policy is to use a full complement of Flight Attendants anytime one Flight Attendant is required (14 CFR 91.533).

q: Who may be carried as passengers on a Part 91 flight operated without Flight Attendants?
a: Passengers are restricted to Alaska Air Group employees, unless authorization for non-employees is received from the Director of Operations, FODO, or NRFO Management.

src.quote: Passengers on Part 91 flights without Flight Attendants will be restricted to Alaska Air Group employees
src.note: Non-employees require authorization from the DO, FODO, or NRFO Management.

q: On a Part 91 non-revenue operation, how many Flight Attendants are required for more than 19 but less than 51 passengers?
a: One (1) Flight Attendant.

src.quote: more than 19 but less than 51 passengers – 1
src.note: The full scale: 19 or less – 0; 19 to under 51 – 1; more than 50 but less than 101 – 2; more than 100 – 2 (+1 for each unit of 50).

q: On a Part 91 non-revenue operation, how many Flight Attendants are required with more than 100 passengers on board?
a: Two (2), plus one additional for each unit of 50 passengers.

src.quote: more than 100 passengers on board – 2 (+1 each unit of 50 passengers)
src.note: This scaling applies to positioning and non-revenue misc operations on all-passenger aircraft.

q: Besides crewmembers, name persons who may be carried on a Part 121 NRFO flight without Flight Attendants when approved.
a: Essential Company employees, an FAA Air Carrier Inspector performing official duties, an NTSB official performing official duties, and persons handling or essential to cargo on NRFO cargo-only flights.

src.quote: FAA Air Carrier Inspector performing official duties
src.note: Requires approval by the Director of Operations or NRFO Management designee (14 CFR 121.583). Any other passenger triggers the full FA complement.

q: What is a Positioning Flight?
a: A flight conducted with an airworthy aircraft flown from one destination to another under 14 CFR Part 91 with no revenue passengers or cargo; it can be for maintenance, charter, scheduling, etc.

src.quote: operated under 14 CFR Part 91 with no revenue passengers or cargo
src.note: A positioning flight delivers the empty aircraft to where a charter begins or back into scheduled service after the charter is over.

q: Which Ops Spec authorizes the Special Flight Permit Ferry, and what does it provide?
a: Maintenance Ops Spec D084 is the Special Flight Permit with Continuous Authorization to Conduct Ferry Flights.

src.quote: Maintenance Ops Spec D084 is the Special Flight Permit with Continuous Authorization to Conduct Ferry Flights
src.note: Section references 14 CFR 21.197 and GPM 05-00-05. The permit authorizes flying an aircraft that may not meet applicable airworthiness requirements.

q: May passengers or cargo be carried on a Special Flight Permit Ferry?
a: No. The flight shall not have passengers or cargo.

src.quote: The flight shall not have passengers or cargo.
src.note: If issued without limitations, the flight is limited to Flight Crew, Flight Attendants, and Maintenance Crew.

q: Can MELs be applied to a flight on a Special Flight Permit, and is ETOPS PDC/PDSC required?
a: Yes, MELs may be applied to flights on a Special Flight Permit. ETOPS PDC/PDSC is not required, but aircraft fluid levels will be inspected and serviced as required.

src.quote: MELs may be applied to flights on a Special Flight Permit.
src.note: Certain MEL Remarks/Exceptions and Operations Procedures may not apply, except for ER operations/ETOPS and flight level restrictions.

q: Does an A330 require a Maintenance Check Flight after a double-engine change, and which group is it?
a: Yes. A 787/A330/A321 flight after a double-engine change is a Group 2 Maintenance Check Flight, which must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot.

src.ref: FOM 16.3.2.2, Classification of Maintenance Check Flights
src.quote: A 787/A330/A321 flight after a double-engine change. (717 double engine change does not require a Maintenance Check Flight provided both engines have undergone test cell runs.)
src.note: Group 2 checks major systems or components to determine airworthiness and may require emergency, abnormal, or special procedures in flight.

q: What are Group 1 and Group 2 Maintenance Check Flights also called?
a: A Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight is also referred to as an 'evaluation flight'; a Group 2 Maintenance Check Flight is also referred to as a 'test flight'.

src.ref: FOM 16.3.2.2, Classification of Maintenance Check Flights
src.quote: Group 1 Maintenance Check Flights, also referred to as an “evaluation flight,” are conducted for the purpose of verifying whether maintenance repairs have successfully corrected a specific aircraft problem.
src.note: Group 1 uses normal FCOM procedures; Group 2 involves specialized training and may use emergency, abnormal, or special procedures.

q: Who may crew a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight, and who is prohibited?
a: It may be flown by a line Captain and a First Officer. A 'High-Minimums Captain' or 'Restricted First Officer' is prohibited from flying a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight.

src.ref: FOM 16.3.2.2, Classification of Maintenance Check Flights
src.quote: A “High-Minimums Captain” or “Restricted First Officer” is prohibited from flying a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight.
src.note: A Group 1 flight is not considered a 'test flight'; the crew is not trained or qualified as test pilots. Group 2 must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot.

q: What two DD Forms is Alaska Airlines issued for use of military airfields, and by whom?
a: DD Form 2401 (Civil Aircraft Landing Permit) and DD Form 2400 (Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance), issued by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps.

src.ref: FOM 16.1.12 - Military Civil Aircraft Landing Permits and Certificate of Insurance
src.quote: Alaska Airlines is issued DD Form 2401, Civil Aircraft Landing Permit, and DD Form 2400, Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps.
src.note: A second AF DD Form 2401 authorizes use of all US Air Force Aviation Facilities worldwide for government charters and contract flights (including AMC).

q: Rev 125 change: where does the FOM now list the specific military bases Alaska Airlines may use?
a: It does not. Rev 125 deleted the per-service base lists (former 16.1.12.1, .2 and .3), including the Bucholz AAF exception. Use of US military installations is limited to those specifically authorized in the approved DD Form 2401.

src.ref: FOM 16.1.12 - Military Civil Aircraft Landing Permits and Certificate of Insurance
src.quote: Alaska Airlines is issued DD Form 2401, Civil Aircraft Landing Permit, and DD Form 2400, Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps.
src.note: The Captain is responsible for knowledge of the limitations in the DD forms; they are located on the EFB in Comply365.

q: How many Maintenance Logbook entries are required for a Special Flight Permit, and what does each describe?
